_README: Approach variants — Mount Baker / Mount Shuksan / far-north Cascades, 2026-08-19. 42 routes, 45 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
`area` on every entry was READ FROM THE LIVE ROW (routes.area_id), not typed from the route name. Three ids in this
batch carry no peak name at all — wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner and wa_sw_couloir_and_face are both MOUNT SHUKSAN,
and wa_ruth_icy_traverse is filed under MOUNT RUTH although the climbing it describes finishes on Icy Peak. A
name-shaped id is not evidence of which peak you are on.
Scope was the peaks named in the request plus the alpine peaks the catalog files beside them in the same subtree
(usa.washington.wa_northwest.wa_shuksan_baker_neighbors): Hadley, Bearpaw, The Pleiades, Mount Herman, Mount Ann,
Table Mountain, Little Sister, Cinderella and Skookum. 51 routes in those areas had an EMPTY approach_variants;
42 are written here and 9 were deliberately skipped — see _SKIPPED.
TWO REQUESTED PEAKS DO NOT EXIST IN THE CATALOG and so could not be covered: Canadian Border Peak (correctly —
it is in British Columbia and out of scope) and Church Mountain (a real Mount Baker Highway peak with a lookout;
it has no area row at all). Yellow Aster Butte likewise has no area of its own — its trailhead is the one the
Tomyhoi Peak route uses, and that is where it appears here.
Contamination rejected during research, recorded so it is not re-introduced:
- AMERICAN Border Peak (7,998 ft, Washington) and CANADIAN Border Peak (2,375 m, British Columbia) sit about a
kilometre apart across the international line and share the phrase 'Border Peak' in nearly every trip report
that mentions either. Only sources describing the approach from Twin Lakes, High Pass and the Gargett Mine —
i.e. the WASHINGTON side — were used. Nothing from the Chilliwack/Slesse side was used for any field.
- There are at least four 'Twin Sisters' in the western United States and one more in Colorado at 13,000 ft that
the search results surfaced repeatedly. Every Twin Sisters source used here is anchored to the Middle Fork
Nooksack River, Mosquito Lake Road, Orsino Creek or Green Creek, which no other Twin Sisters has.
- 'Goat Mountain' is one of the commonest peak names in Washington. The one used here is the Class 2-3 peak on
Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32), reached by Goat Mountain Trail #673 from a trailhead ~2.5 miles up FR-32.
- 'Ruth' appears three times in this region alone: Ruth Mountain (Nooksack), Ruth Creek (the valley the Hannegan
Pass trail follows) and Ruth Peak in the Olympics — a separate catalog row another agent is covering. Nothing
was carried between them. There is also a Ruth Glacier in Alaska, which several searches returned.
- 'Lake Ann' is a name this catalog has already been burned on: the audit that found Black Peak carrying Mount
Baker's Lake Ann is on record. Two Lake Anns are in play in this batch — the one on SR-542 below Artist Point
(Shuksan, Mount Ann) is the correct one for everything written here.
- Mount Lincoln in the Olympics (wa_mount_lincoln) is a DIFFERENT peak from Lincoln Peak on Baker
(wa_lincoln_peak). Only the Baker one is in this batch, and it was matched by coordinate, not by name.
No time, distance or gain figure is averaged. Where two sources disagreed, the field is omitted.
_confidence values used here: 'corroborated' (two or more independent published sources agree on the base),
'single-source' (one published source plus the route row's own columns), 're-homed' (the material comes from
the route row's OWN approach / descent_text / climbing_route prose and no external URL was captured for it —
nothing was researched into these, and no source is claimed), and 'thin' (the base is real but under-published;
the entry says so in its own baseFinding).
Every URL in a _sources list was actually retrieved during this pass. Thirteen rows initially carried
pattern-guessed URLs; those were removed rather than shipped, because a plausible-looking wrong citation is
worse than none.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Ridge Trail #605 to the moraine, then the lower Boulder Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jul. This is a short-season route: the Boulder shrinks and breaks up early, and by August the crevasse field that is walkable in June is a maze
approach_variants.notes:
From the Boulder Ridge Trailhead at the end of FR-1131 off Baker Lake Road (about 2,700 ft — the lowest trailhead of any Baker route, which is where the 7,000+ ft of gain comes from), follow Boulder Ridge Trail #605. The first two miles are nearly flat through old clear-cut and timber and end at a boggy clearing at the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary; the maintained tread effectively stops there.

Beyond it the route is a steep, unmaintained boot path up heather. Around 4,700 ft it crosses a Class 3 rock band, which parties have sometimes found protected by a fixed line left by an earlier team — treat any fixed line as unknown gear, not as trail furniture.

Above the rock band the path gains the crest of a lateral moraine and follows it. Between the meadow and the basalt cliff, stay on or near the moraine crest north of Boulder Creek: the game trails here drop toward the creek and lead nowhere useful.

Camp is on the ridge. Two elevations are published for it and they do not agree — see _DEFECTS — so plan to camp where the ridge runs out into snow rather than at a number.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MORAINE CREST IS THE HANDRAIL, AND THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE IT DIES. Everything from the rock band upward is a walk along a single narrow spine of moraine with the drop into Boulder Creek on one side. In cloud you do not need to see anything: keep the crest under your feet and keep the creek noise on the same side of you the whole way. If the ground under you goes flat and broad, or you are suddenly walking with the creek on the other side, you have come off the moraine and are on the game trails below it.

ARRIVAL: the ridge runs out into snow and ice near 6,300 ft, and that transition — trail-and-heather to glacier — is the base of the route. There is nothing subtle about it; the ground stops being walkable in boots.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTE FROM THIS CAMP, and it matters because both start from the same spot: this route stays ON THE GLACIER. The Boulder-Park Cleaver route crosses the lower glacier northwest to the toe of a rock cleaver and gets onto rock. If you find yourself walking toward a rock rib and looking for a place to step off the ice, you are on the cleaver route, not this one. This route goes up the ice.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: contouring so far northwest that the Park Glacier headwall comes into view above you. That is the neighbouring aspect and its own set of routes.
hazards: A Class 3 rock band around 4,700 ft on an unmaintained boot path, sometimes with an unknown fixed line on it
Losing the moraine crest onto game trails that drop to Boulder Creek
A crevasse field that opens fast — this route has one of the shortest usable seasons on the mountain
Rockfall from the buttress near 9,300 ft on the upper mountain, on the way down as well as up
7,000 ft of gain from the lowest trailhead on the peak, so a late turnaround is a long descent in the dark

approach_variants.name: Boulder Ridge Trail #605 to ridge camp, then across the lower Boulder Glacier to the toe of the cleaver
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Aug — a longer usable window than the pure glacier line beside it, because the cleaver stays climbable after the ice below it has broken up
approach_variants.notes:
The drive and the walk in are identical to the Boulder Glacier route: Baker Lake Road to FR-1130, then FR-1131 to the Boulder Ridge Trailhead near 2,700 ft, and Trail #605 for about two flat miles through clear-cut and timber to the boggy clearing at the wilderness boundary.

Above that the user path climbs steep heather and takes a Class 3 rock step — the one parties have found with a fixed line on it — to a camp on the ridge where it meets snow and ice. A second, higher camp exists on a flat shelf sheltered by the cleaver itself around 7,500 ft, which shortens summit day considerably and is the reason some parties carry over.

From camp the day begins with a glacier crossing rather than a glacier climb: cross the lower Boulder heading northwest to the toe of the cleaver, then follow the cleaver up to just below a large rock buttress near 9,300 ft, where several finishes are possible.

This is Joe Morovits's 1894 line, and it is a different climb from the Boulder Glacier route despite sharing a trailhead, a camp and a name — see _DEFECTS for the first-ascent muddle between the two rows.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A ROCK RIB THAT RISES OUT OF THE GLACIER, AND YOU FIND IT BY BEARING NORTHWEST OFF CAMP AND STOPPING WHEN THE ICE ENDS. That is the whole test and it works blind: from the ridge camp the crossing is a short one, the bearing is northwest, and the thing you are walking toward is the only rock rib coming down into the glacier on that side. Walk until the ice runs into rock. Do not look for a summit.

CONFIRM IT: at the toe you should be able to get off the ice and onto rock without climbing anything — the cleaver's foot is a walk-on, not a step. If you are standing under a wall you have to climb to get established, you are somewhere else on the glacier margin.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE ROUTE THAT SHARES THIS CAMP: the Boulder Glacier route never leaves the ice. If you are still roped up on glacier at 8,000 ft with no rock under you, you are on that route rather than this one. Conversely if you are on a rock spine with glacier falling away on BOTH sides, you are on the cleaver and you are right.

WHAT TOO HIGH LOOKS LIKE: the cleaver runs into a large rock buttress around 9,300 ft. That buttress is a decision point, not a base — it is where the finishes diverge, and if you have reached it you are 3,600 ft above the start of the route.
hazards: A Class 3 rock step on the approach with an unknown fixed line sometimes in place
Crevasse navigation on the short crossing of the lower Boulder to the toe, which changes year to year
Rockfall exposure near the 9,300 ft buttress, going up and coming down
The 7,500 ft high camp sits on the mountain with no bail-out short of reversing the cleaver
8,000 ft of cumulative gain — the biggest gain of any Baker route because the trailhead is the lowest

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Creek from the old lodge site, up the White Salmon Glacier to the dividing shoulder
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug. Earlier the valley is snow-covered and simpler but the true North Face above you sheds avalanches; later the crevasses on the White Salmon are open and the lower valley is alder
approach_variants.notes:
Get the free backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center on the way in — it is required, not advisory. Then continue up the Mount Baker Highway to the pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site, walk round the gate, and follow the old roadbed roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut.

From the road-end, with adequate snow cover, drop northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Roped travel usually begins at the toe, and the crevasse hazard grows through the season.

Ascend glacier and moraine to a bivy below the first rock and ice barrier. Published bivy elevations for this route disagree by around a thousand feet — see _DEFECTS — so the honest instruction is to camp at the rock outcrops on the eastern edge of the White Salmon, where the ridge meets the face, rather than at a number.

The on-file text used to group this route with the Nooksack and Ruth Creek side of the mountain. It does not belong there: route-specific sources put the Hanging Glacier and North Face approach in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley east of Price Lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PRICE LAKE MUST STAY BELOW YOU AND TO YOUR WEST, AND THAT IS THE TEST. From the bivy the day is a traverse climber's LEFT, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier. In cloud you will not see the summit and you do not need to: the lake is the reference and it belongs on your left-hand side, downhill.

ARRIVAL: you are at the base of the technical climbing when you reach the SHOULDER — the snow-and-ice rib that divides the White Salmon cirque from the Price Glacier cirque. It is the only place on this traverse where the ground stops being a sidehill and becomes a defined rib with a cirque falling away on each side. Stand on it and you should be able to look down into two separate basins.

THE ERROR THAT KILLS PEOPLE HERE IS DRIFTING LEFT, and it is worth stating as a hard rule: stay RIGHT during the traverse. Going further left puts you onto the true North Face, which sheds avalanches frequently, especially early season. Left feels like progress toward the mountain and is the wrong direction.

AFTER 500 FT OF TRAVERSE the line goes UP, on a firn-and-ice finger west of the upper hanging glacier. If you are still traversing horizontally after a long way, you have gone past the finger and are running out under the face.
hazards: Frequent avalanches off the true North Face onto the traverse, worst in early season
Serac fall from the hanging glacier itself, which is described as very active
Open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier that grow through the season
Brush and alder in the lower White Salmon valley once the snowline recedes
A traverse with no easy retreat once committed, and a bivy on the mountain

approach_variants.name: Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide, then down the White Salmon Glacier to the base
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug, once the Lake Ann trail is out from under snow
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative used by parties who would rather start from the standard trailhead than from the White Salmon roadbed: from the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, climb the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Lower Curtis Glacier, then descend about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverse the northwest rib to reach the foot of the Hanging Glacier.

It is longer in vertical terms because it climbs to a camp and then gives back a thousand feet, and it commits you to regaining that thousand feet on the way out if you return the same way. Its advantage is a maintained trail to a known camp instead of a valley bushwhack, and it does not require the White Salmon roadbed to be walkable.

No trailhead-to-base time is given for this variant; published figures for it vary too much to quote one.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE FROM ABOVE, SO THE TEST IS INVERTED — YOU ARE LOOKING FOR THE BOTTOM OF A DESCENT, NOT THE TOP OF A CLIMB. From the Lower Curtis bivy you drop roughly 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier. Stop descending when the ground lets you traverse northeast onto the northwest rib; if you keep going down the White Salmon you end up in the valley the other variant walked up, and you will have thrown away the whole approach.

THE RIB IS THE MARKER. The northwest rib is a defined feature between the White Salmon and the Hanging Glacier, and once you are on it the foot of the Hanging Glacier is the next thing you meet.

CONFIRM WITH THE SAME TEST THE OTHER VARIANT USES: from the base of the climbing, Price Lake should be below you and to the west, and you should be standing on the shoulder that separates the White Salmon cirque from the Price cirque, with a basin on each side of you.

AND THE SAME HARD RULE APPLIES: do not drift left onto the true North Face. It avalanches, and arriving from this side does not change that.
hazards: A 1,000 ft descent that must be re-climbed on the return if you reverse this variant
Winnie's Slide, which is sometimes rappelled rather than downclimbed when icy
Crevasses on both the Lower Curtis and the White Salmon
Avalanche exposure from the true North Face during the traverse
Committing to a route whose descent normally exits a different valley from the one you started in

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Creek roadbed, then the ridgecrest opposite the ski area
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. This is the more direct of the two options and it is a bushwhack, so it wants the ground clear rather than snow-covered
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR-542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. This first stretch is common to both options.

The direct option then drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest DIRECTLY OPPOSITE THE SKI AREA, then follows that crest to the base of the mountain's north side.

This is a long Cascade adventure route rather than a line with a bootpack: bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel, all in one day. It was climbed in 2007 by a party who took sixteen hours on the 1,300 ft arête alone, having started from the White Salmon Glacier.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SKI AREA IS THE ONE THING YOU CAN SEE FROM ANYWHERE, AND IT IS THE AIMING MARK. The crest you want is the one directly opposite the ski area across White Salmon Creek. Cross the creek, climb, and stop when you are on a crest with the ski area behind you and level with you. In flat light that back-bearing is more reliable than anything ahead of you, because the ski area's cut runs and lift lines are the only man-made shape in the drainage.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROUTE ITSELF: the crest is a ramp, not the climb. Follow it until it runs into the mountain's north side, and the arête proper is the pillar the crest delivers you to. It is roughly 1,300 ft of climbing above that point.

DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE ROUTES EITHER SIDE OF IT: this is a ROCK PILLAR, not a glacier and not a snow face. If the ground in front of you at the base is a glacier you are looking at the White Salmon; if it is a broad snow-and-ice face you are looking at the North Face. The northwest arête is the pillar between them, and the first ground you touch on it is rock.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the valley past the point where the opposite crest is climbable puts you on the other variant — up the valley to the lower White Salmon Glacier. That is a legitimate approach, but it is a different one, and mixing the two mid-way leaves you sidehilling.
hazards: Bushwhacking with no tread, where a wrong drainage costs a day
Runout climbing on loose rock high on the arête
Moderate alpine ice and extensive glacier travel on the same outing as the rock
A very long day: the first-ascent party took sixteen hours on the arête itself
A descent that exits down the upper and lower White Salmon Glacier rather than reversing the climb

approach_variants.name: Up the White Salmon valley to the lower glacier, then onto the crest
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative from the same parking: continue up the road as far as it goes, then travel off-trail up the valley until open slopes allow access to the lower White Salmon Glacier, and gain the crest of the arête from there.

It trades the creek crossing and the direct climb to the crest for more valley travel and a glacier approach. Parties choosing between the two are choosing between bushwhack-then-ridge and valley-then-glacier; both are documented and neither is a shortcut.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GLACIER IS THE HANDRAIL, AND YOU LEAVE IT WHEN THE ROCK STARTS. Stay in the valley until the slopes open enough to walk onto the lower White Salmon Glacier, then work up the glacier with the arête's rock on your side and step onto it where the two meet.

THE TEST THAT SETTLES IT is the same one the direct variant uses, from the other direction: at the base of this route you are on ROCK, with the White Salmon Glacier on one side of the pillar and the North Face ground on the other. If you can still see glacier on both sides of you, you have not stepped onto the arête yet.

WHAT DROPPING TOO LOW LOOKS LIKE: if the valley narrows and you are still in trees and brush with no open slope, you have not gone far enough up-valley to reach the glacier access, and pushing sideways onto the mountain from there puts you on steep vegetated ground below the pillar rather than at its foot.

AND THE ORIENTATION CHECK: the descent for this route comes down the upper and then the lower White Salmon Glacier and deposits you back in this drainage. If your intended base is somewhere you could not plausibly walk back to down a glacier on this side, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.
hazards: Extensive glacier travel with crevasse hazard on the lower White Salmon
Off-trail valley travel with no tread and brush low down
Loose rock and runout climbing on the arête above
Complex route-finding described by the first-ascent party as one of the route's defining features
No quick retreat: the descent is a separate glacier descent, not a reverse of the climb

approach_variants.name: Shannon Ridge and the Sulphide Glacier to the notch on the southeast ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Sulphide is walkable and the rock is out from under snow
approach_variants.notes:
From the Shannon Ridge Trailhead, climb east-northeast up Shannon Ridge and onto the Sulphide Glacier — the standard Shuksan approach, and the same one the Sulphide Glacier route uses. Most parties camp on the large flat plateau around 6,400 ft, which is the usual staging point for summit day.

The snow between roughly 5,400 and 6,400 ft is where visibility bites: it is featureless open ground and parties report it as the tricky stretch in reduced visibility. Above camp the upper Sulphide is mellow, with a few small crevasses that are generally stepped over.

This route then leaves the standard finish. Where the Sulphide Glacier route walks to the foot of the summit pyramid and takes its Class 3-4 gully, this one gains the ridge at a notch further east and climbs about six pitches of well-featured 5.3 rock to the top.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IS THE ROUTE, AND YOU CAN FEEL IT RATHER THAN SEE IT. Gaining the southeast ridge happens at a PROMINENT NOTCH at the top of the upper Sulphide. In cloud, work up the glacier until the snow stops rising and you can step onto rock at a low point in the ridgeline with ground falling away on the far side. A notch you can stand in with air behind you is the arrival; a rock wall in front of you with snow still under your feet is not.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE STANDARD ROUTE, and it is the mistake this entry exists to prevent: the Sulphide Glacier route's finish is a FOURTH-CLASS GULLY up the summit pyramid, and it is the line almost everyone on the mountain is walking toward. If you find yourself queueing at the bottom of a gully with a bootpack into it, you are at the standard finish, not at this route's start. This route gains a ridge crest, not a gully.

SECOND TEST, ON THE ROPE: the climbing here is six pitches of extremely well-featured rock that parties describe as easy in boots, with limited protection and severe exposure on BOTH sides of the crest. If your first pitch is a gully with walls either side of you rather than a crest with air either side of you, you have started in the wrong place. Exposure on both sides is the confirmation.

WHAT WALKING PAST IT LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the Sulphide beyond the notch brings you under the summit pyramid's south side, where the standard gully is. That is the descent for this route — the same gully is rappelled on the way down — so recognising it does not mean you are lost, but it does mean you have gone past the start.
hazards: Featureless snow between 5,400 and 6,400 ft that is genuinely hard to navigate in reduced visibility
Limited protection on well-featured but sparsely protectable 5.3 rock
Severe exposure on both sides of the crest on the final steps
Crevasses on the Sulphide, small but present
A descent that rappels a gully shared with the standard route, so parties above you are a rockfall source

approach_variants.name: Lake Ann, then right onto the Lower Curtis Glacier to its upper southeast corner
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, about a mile below Artist Point at roughly 4,770 ft, take Lake Ann Trail #600 to the lake and on toward the Fisher Chimneys.

Before the Chimneys, traverse RIGHT — east — onto the Lower Curtis Glacier and follow it up to the upper southeast corner of the glacier basin. This is where the technical climbing starts, at the foot of the icefall.

The descent for this route goes back via the Hourglass and the Upper Curtis to the Shuksan Arm — the Fisher Chimneys descent — so the day is a loop rather than a reverse, and the whole thing is commonly cited at around eight hours round trip from Lake Ann.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FISHER CHIMNEYS ARE THE JUNCTION, AND THE INSTRUCTION IS ONE WORD: RIGHT. Everyone else on this trail is going up the Chimneys. You go right, east, onto the Lower Curtis. If you are climbing a chimney system, you have missed the turn.

ARRIVAL: keep going up the glacier until you are in the UPPER SOUTHEAST CORNER of the basin — the deepest, highest inside corner of the cirque, where the glacier runs out against the mountain. The base is at the foot of the ICEFALL. In cloud, the corner is found by feel: keep the rock on your right and climb until the glacier stops going anywhere.

THE FIRST HUNDRED FEET CONFIRMS IT, and this is the strongest test on the route. The climbing opens with about 100 ft of steep snow leading to a LARGE TRANSVERSE CREVASSE running across the line. That crevasse is unmistakable, it is at the start rather than in the middle, and it is the thing that tells you you are in the right corner. Above it is roughly 300 ft of steep ice and snow to the base of the headwall.

WHAT BEING IN THE WRONG CORNER LOOKS LIKE: if the first 100 ft of snow leads to open glacier rather than to a crevasse spanning your line, you are still out in the basin. If the ground above the first steep snow is a rock wall you cannot get above in 300 ft, you are too far east against the headwall proper.

AND THE SEQUENCE ABOVE, worth carrying because it double-checks the start: at the base of the headwall the route traverses LEFT to a weakness, 100 ft of fourth class to a ledge, then left again around a corner onto a buttress. A route that never traverses left is not this one.
hazards: A large transverse crevasse across the line in the first 100 ft
Icefall exposure at the foot of the upper southeast corner
About 1,000 ft of easy fifth-class buttress climbing with alpine protection
A descent by a different line (Hourglass and Upper Curtis to the Shuksan Arm), so the way home is not the way up
Crevasses on the Lower Curtis on the approach traverse

approach_variants.name: Ruth Creek washout, Nooksack Cirque, Price Lake moraine and the ridge to the 5,900 ft slab bivy
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. Earlier the river is high and the couloir is safer; later the river drops but the couloir bakes and sheds rock
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mount Baker Highway, turn left onto Nooksack River Road (FS-32) immediately before the Nooksack River bridge, about 13 miles past Glacier. Stay left at 0.5 miles, right at 1.4 miles, and park at the washout at 2.3 miles from the highway, by Ruth Creek at about 2,156 ft.

Walk the abandoned road beyond the washout for two miles to the Nooksack Cirque trailhead at 2,550 ft. Ford the Nooksack. There is a recorded log crossing near N48.87097 W121.61267 — new logs get swept away every year, so treat the coordinate as where to start looking rather than as a bridge.

Go up the forested mountainside east of the creek, starting on the west bank of Price Creek until a good log turns up. Continue to the moraine above Price Lake at 3,911 ft, then follow the ridgeline BETWEEN the Price and East Nooksack Glaciers up to a rock slab bivouac around 5,900 ft.

From the bivy, get onto the glacier, traverse climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, then drop down and work onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier.

This route belongs to Nooksack Tower and not to Mount Shuksan — it was merged from a duplicate Shuksan row earlier in this sweep, and the Price Glacier route on Shuksan is a different climb sharing much of the same ground.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BERGSCHRUND AT ROUGHLY 6,500 FT IS THE BASE, AND THE COULOIR ABOVE IT IS THE ONLY ONE. Beckey and Schmidtke's own account of the first ascent puts them at the bergschrund at the foot of the final north face at 6,500 ft, with 800 ft of 50-degree ice couloir above. That is the arrival: a schrund, then a single steep couloir that guards the Tower.

THE RIDGE BETWEEN THE TWO GLACIERS IS THE HANDRAIL. From the Price Lake moraine you climb a rib with the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. In cloud you do not need the Tower: keep a glacier on each side of you and go up. If you only have ice on one side, you have come off the rib.

THE SADDLE IS THE HINGE, AND IT IS COUNTERINTUITIVE. From the bivy the traverse is climber's RIGHT to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, and then you DROP DOWN onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. Losing height here feels wrong and is correct. A party that refuses to descend off the saddle stays high on the wrong side and never reaches the couloir.

CONFIRM AT THE SCHRUND: the couloir starts around 50 degrees and steepens to about 60 at the top, with a single 70-degree step where it hits rock. If your line eases off rather than steepens, it is not the couloir. Parties have found the schrund hollow and swung WIDE LEFT to avoid it entirely — that is a known variation, not a sign you are lost.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the Price Glacier past the Tower's couloir puts you on the Price Glacier route on SHUKSAN, which is a different mountain's climb reached from the same basin. Nooksack Tower is the freestanding tower below and north of Shuksan's summit; if the ground above your couloir keeps going for thousands of feet rather than ending on a tower in about 1,200 ft of fourth class, you are on Shuksan.
hazards: Fording the Nooksack on logs that are swept away and replaced yearly
Rockfall down the couloir, recorded on the first ascent and in every account since
A hollow bergschrund that has forced parties to swing wide left
A descent of roughly ten 60 m rappels off gear you build yourself — fixed anchors here should not be trusted
Parties routinely still on the couloir or the lower approach after dark; one fast team recorded 21 hours car to car

approach_variants.name: The Beckey approach as far as the Price Lake moraine, then the East Nooksack Glacier instead of the Price
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Beckey-Schmidtke route as far as the moraine above Price Lake: Ruth Creek washout, two miles of abandoned road to the Nooksack Cirque trailhead, the Nooksack ford, the forested slope east of the creek, and the moraine at 3,911 ft.

The two routes then part company at the top of the rib. Instead of continuing toward the Price Glacier, traverse onto the EAST NOOKSACK Glacier and climb to the base of the south face, somewhere between about 6,500 and 7,000 ft, where the wall rises directly out of the glacier.

Several variations exist depending on snow and ice conditions, and the climb starts on the RIGHT side of the face. It was first climbed in July 2002 and it is a much longer rock route than the Beckey line — twelve pitches against ten.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM IS WHICH GLACIER YOU END UP ON, AND THE ANSWER IS THE EAST ONE. The rib above Price Lake has the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. The Beckey route commits to the Price. This route commits to the East Nooksack. That single decision, made at the top of the rib, is the difference between a north-face ice couloir and a south-face rock climb, and once you are on the wrong glacier nothing further down the day will correct it.

THE ASPECT SETTLES IT IN FOG, WITH NO VISIBILITY AT ALL. This route faces SOUTH. If the wall in front of you is in shade all morning and holds ice, you are under the north face and on the Beckey route's ground. If the wall catches the sun and is dry rock, you are where you meant to be.

ARRIVAL: the south face rises DIRECTLY ABOVE THE GLACIER — there is no intervening basin, moraine or approach slope. You walk on ice until the ice ends at the wall. That directness is the marker; a wall you reach after scrambling up talus is not this one.

AND THE START IS ON THE RIGHT. Having reached the foot of the face, the climb begins on its RIGHT side. A party that starts up the middle or the left of a twelve-pitch face on a rarely climbed tower has committed to unknown ground with a technical descent waiting for them.

DESCENT NOTE THAT DOUBLE-CHECKS THE START: the first-ascent party did not reverse this face. They descended the standard north-face route on the front of the tower, i.e. over the top and down the other side. If you are planning to rappel your line of ascent, you are planning something nobody has recorded.
hazards: Choosing the wrong glacier at the top of the Price Lake rib, which is unrecoverable that day
Twelve pitches on a rarely repeated face with variations that depend on conditions
A descent by a different route on the opposite side of the tower
The same Nooksack ford and log-crossing problem as the Beckey route
Crevasses on the East Nooksack Glacier

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trail #677 and the Coleman Glacier to the bench beneath the north faces
approach_variants.season: Roughly Oct-May. This is a cold-season route: it wants the north faces frozen, and it avalanches after new snow
approach_variants.notes:
From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR-39) near 3,700 ft, follow Trail #677 about two miles through forest, over a plank bridge on Grouse Creek and across one avalanche path below Hogsback that can hold debris and running water in warm conditions. The trail breaks out of trees near the Coleman icefall viewpoint around 4,900-5,000 ft — the last reliable running water before the moraine.

Gain the lateral moraine and the well-worn Coleman-Deming boot track, staying on or near the moraine crest before dropping onto ice. Rope up here.

Contour and ascend the Coleman climber's RIGHT — northeast — toward the bench beneath Colfax's north faces, staying low and left around the large crevasse that guards the direct line. Parties in good booting conditions commonly reach the bench in three to four and a half hours from the car.

FOUR ROUTES SHARE THIS BENCH, and telling them apart is the whole point of the baseFinding below.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM LEFT TO RIGHT AS YOU STAND ON THE BENCH FACING THE FACE, THE FOUR LINES ARE: KIMCHI SUICIDE VOLCANO, POLISH ROUTE, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. Learn that order before you leave the car. It is the only thing that separates a WI4 from a WI6 in the dark, and all four start within a few hundred metres of each other above the same bergschrund.

COSLEY-HOUSTON IS THE SECOND FROM THE RIGHT AND THE EASIEST LINE ON THE FACE. Cross or tunnel the bergschrund and go UP AND RIGHT of the Polish Route. If you have gone left of the continuous ice line up the middle of the face, you are on the Polish Route and you are on a grade harder than you came for.

THE POSITIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE STRONG ONE: above the schrund this route opens with a LOW-ANGLE ICE RAMP leading up to the base of an obvious crux pillar. Low-angle first, pillar second. If your first ground above the schrund is steep — a continuous fat ice line that stands up immediately — you are on the Polish. If it is rock with face holds and mixed moves rather than ice, you are far left on Kimchi.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE CRUX OBSTACLE OF THE APPROACH, not a formality. It is frequently overhanging and in lean years it has needed a mixed traverse in from the right. Cross it early, before the north-facing slopes see any sun.

WHAT BEING TOO FAR RIGHT LOOKS LIKE: Ford's Theatre is hidden from the standard approach, tucked in a cleft around the right side of a buttress. If you have walked right until the face disappears behind a buttress, you have gone past Cosley-Houston entirely.
hazards: An overhanging bergschrund that is the crux obstacle of the approach in lean years
Avalanche on this aspect after any new snow — do not climb it on a loaded slope
Crevasses on the Coleman, including one large one that guards the direct line to the bench
Sun-warming of the north faces later in the day, so the schrund must be crossed early
A glacier descent that multiple parties specifically warn against doing after dark

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then the schrund guarding the middle of the face
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-May
approach_variants.notes:
The trailhead and the lower approach are the same as Cosley-Houston: Heliotrope Ridge trailhead near 3,700 ft, Trail #677 for roughly two miles through forest, water at the moraine/treeline break, then the standard Coleman-Deming boot track onto the glacier and climber's right toward the bench under Colfax's north faces. Rope up for crevasse travel on the glacier.

Parties leaving the car around 3:30 am with a well-consolidated track have reported the bench in under three hours; that figure varies enormously with snowpack and traffic and should not be planned on.

Gear up on the bench. The bergschrund here guards the Polish Route directly, is frequently large and overhanging, and has required parties to traverse right and tunnel through overhanging snow and ice to gain the first ice pitch.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ON THIS FACE: KIMCHI, POLISH, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. The Polish Route is the SECOND FROM THE LEFT and it takes the OBVIOUS CONTINUOUS ICE LINE UP THE MIDDLE OF THE FACE, just left of and parallel to the Cosley-Houston gully.

THE TEST IS THE ICE ITSELF, AND IT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING THE WHOLE FACE. This is a WI6 — the hardest line here by a wide margin — and above the schrund it stands up immediately. If the first ground above the schrund is a LOW-ANGLE RAMP you can walk up, you are on Cosley-Houston, which is the easiest line on the face and sits immediately to your right. That single difference, ramp versus steep ice off the deck, separates WI4 from WI6 at the moment of committing.

IF THE ROCK MATTERS MORE THAN THE ICE, YOU ARE TOO FAR LEFT. Kimchi Suicide Volcano takes an independent line to the LEFT of this route and is described by its first-ascent party as more of a mixed climb than a pure ice climb, on well-featured rock with plenty of face holds. Continuous ice with no rock moves is the Polish; face holds and mixed ground is Kimchi.

CONFIRM WITH THE SCHRUND: the schrund that guards this route specifically is frequently large and overhanging, and the documented workaround is to traverse RIGHT and tunnel through overhanging snow. If you crossed a schrund comfortably on a snow bridge and walked straight onto easy ground, you have probably crossed at the Cosley-Houston line.

WHY IT MATTERS TO CHECK THE PARALLEL GULLY: the two lines run parallel up the same face, so being one line out does not become obvious until you are committed on steep ice with the wrong rack.
hazards: A large, frequently overhanging bergschrund that has needed tunnelling
WI6 ice on a face that catches afternoon sun despite its northwest aspect
Avalanche on this aspect after new snow — do not do the schrund on a loaded slope
A descent mixing short V-thread rappels with downclimbing, on threads you build yourself
Crevasses on the Coleman on the way out, with the glacier descent flagged as hazardous after dark

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then right around the buttress into the cleft
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr — the first ascent was 20 April 2015 and this is a cold-season ice line
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is shared with Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano: from Glacier, WA up Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, then Trail #677 onto the Coleman Glacier moraine and glacier travel climber's right to the bench beneath Colfax's north face.

What is different about this route begins at the bench rather than before it. Ford's Theatre is the RIGHTMOST of the four lines and it is about 500 ft of AI4+: three pitches of steep ice before the angle relents into steep snow gullies. Belay options after the first pitch are scarce, and the first-ascent party recommended running pitches two and three together to avoid hanging ice-screw belays.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IF YOU CAN SEE YOUR ROUTE FROM THE BENCH, IT IS NOT FORD'S THEATRE. That is the single most useful fact about this climb and it is the one the first-ascent party chose to record: most of the route is HIDDEN during the standard approach to the north face, because it sits in a cleft around the RIGHT side of a buttress. The other three lines are all visible from the approach. This one is not.

SO THE PROCEDURE IS: walk right along the base of the face, past the Cosley-Houston line, until a buttress cuts the face off from view — then go around the right side of that buttress. The route is in the cleft behind it. A climber who stops at the first steep ice they can see has stopped on Cosley-Houston.

LEFT TO RIGHT, THE FOUR LINES ARE: KIMCHI, POLISH, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. This is the far right end of that list, which is why the instruction is always 'keep going'.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: three pitches of sustained steep ice, roughly 500 ft, then the angle eases into snow gullies. Belays are hard to find after the first pitch. If you get a comfortable stance every rope length, or if the route stays steep for far more than 500 ft, you are on something else.

WHAT BEING SHORT LOOKS LIKE: Cosley-Houston starts with a LOW-ANGLE ICE RAMP above the schrund leading to a crux pillar. If you are walking up a ramp, you are one line to the left of where you meant to be — which is a fine route and a different one.
hazards: Sustained AI4+ with almost no belay options after the first pitch
Hanging ice-screw belays if the pitches are not run together
The route is hidden from the approach, so its condition cannot be assessed before committing
Avalanche on this aspect after new snow, and the same overhanging bergschrund problem as the neighbouring lines
Crevasses on the Coleman and a glacier descent that should not be left until after dark

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then the leftmost line on the face
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr — the first ascent was April 2015, in cold-season conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as its three neighbours: Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, Trail #677 through forest to the Coleman Glacier moraine, the Coleman-Deming boot track onto the ice, and climber's right to the bench beneath Colfax's north face. Rope up on the glacier.

The route itself is about 300 m at AI4+ M5 R. Its first-ascent party described it as more of a mixed climb than a pure ice climb, on rock that is well featured with plenty of face holds — which is what the M5 and the R are about.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE LEFTMOST LINE ON THE FACE, AND THE TEST IS WHETHER YOU ARE CLIMBING ROCK. Left to right the four lines are KIMCHI, POLISH, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. Kimchi takes an independent line to the LEFT of the Polish Route, so from the bench you walk left, past the obvious continuous ice line up the middle of the face, and keep going.

THE CHARACTER OF THE GROUND IS THE CONFIRMATION, and it discriminates cleanly against the route next door. The Polish Route is continuous ICE — that is its whole identity, and it is graded WI6 for it. This route is MIXED: the first-ascent account is explicit that it is more mixed than pure ice, and that the rock is well featured with plenty of face holds. So the question to ask at the schrund is not 'which line is this' but 'am I about to use my hands on rock'. If the answer is no, you are on the Polish and on a much harder ice grade than you came for.

THE R IN THE GRADE IS PART OF THE BASE FINDING. This is AI4+ M5 R, and R means the protection is poor enough that a fall has consequences beyond the fall. Being one line right of here — on continuous well-protected ice — is a materially different commitment. Confirm which you are on before the leader is 30 m up.

WHAT BEING TOO FAR RIGHT LOOKS LIKE, all the way across the face: a low-angle ice ramp to a crux pillar is Cosley-Houston, the easiest line here. A route you cannot see at all from the bench, tucked behind a buttress, is Ford's Theatre at the far right end.
hazards: M5 R protection — a graded runout, not an incidental one
300 m of mixed ground with the schrund below it
Avalanche on this aspect after new snow
Crevasses on the Coleman approach and descent
A rarely repeated line, so conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jul. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
approach_variants.notes:
IMPORTANT AND FIRST: the X Couloir is approached from the SOUTH via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38), not from Heliotrope Ridge. Heliotrope serves Lincoln's separate northwest-face line. Getting this wrong puts you on the opposite side of the mountain with a glacier between you and your route.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

ACCESS: as of mid-2026 FR-38 has reported washout damage from the December 2025 floods with no confirmed repair timeline, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGHEST TREES IN THE BASIN ARE THE CAMP, AND THE CAMP IS THE LAST THING YOU CAN NAVIGATE TO. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

DO NOT EXPECT ONE CLEAN COULOIR — THIS IS THE TRAP THE NAME SETS. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the HIGHEST notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

THE SERAC STEP IS THE CONFIRMATION. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

AND THE ASPECT SETTLES THE COARSE ERROR: this route faces SOUTHWEST and you reach it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you have come in from Heliotrope and you are under the other route on this mountain.
hazards: A bergschrund crossing that must be done cold and early
1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all of it above a long runout
FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec - 15 Jun
A gully that funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
A descent that is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge to the Kulshan Cabin site, then high and right on the Coleman beneath the icefall
approach_variants.season: Winter to early spring. The only documented ascent was mid-March, in a lean cold winter — this is an ice objective and it needs the ice to exist
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead on FS Road 39, Trail #677, near Glacier. Follow the trail roughly 2.7-3 miles through old growth and several avalanche-chute creek crossings to the flat former Kulshan Cabin site around 3,200 ft, which is the usual camp and staging area.

From there climb the Hogsback moraine to the toe of the Coleman Glacier and rope up. Where the party heading for the southwest side of the mountain would cut away toward the Thunder Glacier cirque, this route stays HIGHER and further climber's RIGHT — east — on the Coleman, traversing beneath the Coleman icefall to reach the north-facing cirque wedged between Colfax Peak and Lincoln Peak.

That traverse is longer and more exposed than the south-side approach: for a stretch you are directly beneath active serac bands on the upper icefall, so serac collapse is a real objective hazard and an early, cold start matters more here than it does on the other side of the mountain.

NOTE ON THIS ROW: it names one first-ascent party in its fa field and a different, much earlier one in its approach prose. See _DEFECTS. Treat the route's history as unsettled; the ground described is not in doubt.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A CIRQUE WITH A PEAK ON EACH SIDE OF IT, AND THAT IS THE TEST. Lincoln's north face sits in a north-facing cirque WEDGED BETWEEN COLFAX PEAK AND LINCOLN PEAK. You have arrived when the ground you are standing on is enclosed on two sides by rock rising to two separate summits, with the Coleman behind you. One peak above you is not enough; you need the cirque.

THE HANDRAIL IS THE ICEFALL, AND IT IS OVERHEAD RATHER THAN UNDERFOOT. From the Coleman's toe, stay HIGH and go RIGHT, traversing beneath the icefall. Icefall above you on your left is the confirmation you are on the correct traverse; it is also the reason to be there before the sun. If you find yourself descending toward a cirque with no icefall above you, you have cut left toward the Thunder Glacier side and are heading for the southwest face.

THE FACE ITSELF IS ABOUT 1,000 FT AND IT IS ICE. If the wall in front of you is a snow slope you could walk, it is not this route. The historical record for this line is explicit that it demanded ice screws, and modern accounts grade it WI4/AI4+; rime, verglas and bare ice vary hugely by year, so what you find may be harder or easier than the grade but it will not be a scramble.

GO EARLY IN THE SEASON FOR TWO REASONS AT ONCE: the ice is better, and the crevasses on the traverse are better bridged. Those two arguments point the same way, which is unusual and worth using.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG SIDE LOOKS LIKE: open snow basin, sun on your back, trees below you at 6,100 ft. That is the X Couloir approach from Rankin Creek and it is reached from a different road entirely.
hazards: Traversing directly beneath active serac bands on the Coleman icefall
Crevasses on a long, exposed, high traverse of the Coleman
Roughly 1,000 ft of ice and mixed ground with conditions that vary enormously year to year
Loose rock reported on the face, which matters because the descent means building anchors on it
No documented independent descent — parties either reverse the face or traverse to the southwest gully

approach_variants.name: Park Butte Trail and the Railroad Grade moraine to Sandy Camp, then the Easton Glacier to the crater rim
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
From the Park Butte Trailhead at the end of FR-13 near 3,360 ft, follow Park Butte Trail #603 south into Schriebers Meadow. Within the first 0.3-0.4 mile the trail fords Sulfur Creek — braided, silty glacial melt that runs high and fast on warm afternoons, usually rock-hoppable or bridged by a seasonal plank early in the summer.

Beyond the creek the trail climbs through timber and brushy avalanche terrain, crosses more meltwater streams, and switchbacks into Morovitz Meadows about two miles in. At the upper meadow bear RIGHT at the signed Scott Paul Trail #603.1 junction to stay on Park Butte, then take the NEXT RIGHT onto Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 toward Baker Pass. Straight ahead at that second fork goes to the Park Butte lookout instead — a pleasant hike and the wrong one.

Railroad Grade #603.2 climbs onto the crest of the lateral moraine left by the receding Easton Glacier — a uniformly graded ridge, hence the name, with steep drops on both sides in places. Designated camps sit at 2.25-2.75 miles; High Camp is around 3.75 miles and 5,600 ft; Sandy Camp near 5,900 ft is where maintained tread ends.

There is no potable water at the trailhead. Treat from Sulfur or Rocky Creek near the start, or melt at camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MORAINE CREST IS A HANDRAIL YOU CAN FOLLOW BLIND, AND SANDY CAMP IS WHERE IT ENDS. Railroad Grade is exactly what its name says: a narrow, uniformly graded spine with the drop on both sides. In whiteout — which is the normal condition on Baker's south side, where a cloud cap forms on otherwise clear days — you do not navigate on this stretch, you follow the spine. When the maintained tread stops at Sandy Camp near 5,900 ft, you are at the end of the handrail and the start of the route.

FROM THERE THE ROUTE IS CROSS-COUNTRY over snowfields and rocky moraine to the toe of the Easton Glacier. Rope up somewhere around 6,800-7,200 ft depending on conditions. The glacier heading is NORTH, angling slightly WEST toward Sherman Peak, and the standard line stays EAST — climber's right — of the glacier's major crevasse bands.

WAND IT. This is not a hedge; it is standard practice on this route precisely because the crater rim and the moraine crest offer no natural handrail above Sandy Camp and the cloud cap arrives without warning. Route-finding through the crevasse field is the technical crux of the whole approach and it shifts season to season, so your own wands going up are the only reliable line coming down.

ARRIVAL AT SHERMAN PEAK ITSELF: above roughly 9,600-9,800 ft you reach the rim of Sherman Crater, and you will smell it before you see it — active fumaroles vent sulphurous steam, and the rock near them is acid-degraded. That smell is the confirmation that you are at the crater rim and not on the Roman Wall heading for Baker's true summit, which is the other thing this glacier leads to. Stay on the established boot path here and keep gear off the degraded rock.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up past the crater rim onto the steep sustained snow of the Roman Wall means you have left Sherman Peak below you and are climbing Mount Baker.
hazards: A braided glacial ford of Sulfur Creek that runs high on warm afternoons
Exposed drops on both sides of the Railroad Grade moraine crest, worse in wind or on frosty mornings
A crevasse field that is the technical crux of the approach and moves season to season
Baker's characteristic cloud cap and whiteouts on the south side, above the last natural handrail
Active fumaroles and acid-degraded rock at the Sherman Crater rim

approach_variants.name: Cougar Divide Trail #601 and the open ridge northeast to Chowder Ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Oct, once the ridge is out from under snow
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, WA, drive SR-542 east and turn onto Forest Service Road 33; follow about 11 miles of gravel — rough in sections, high-clearance recommended, sedans passable with care — to its end at the Cougar Divide trailhead, with room for eight to ten vehicles. The true trailhead may be roughly a kilometre past where online mapping routes you, so do not stop at the first turnaround that looks right.

Hike Cougar Divide Trail #601 along the ridge to its high point around 5,920 ft. That high point is where maintained tread ends and the route becomes cross-country: continue northeast along the open ridge, crossing near Dobbs Creek, to Chowder Ridge and the foot of Hadley's summit block.

This and the Skyline Divide route are two different walks to the SAME summit block; the beta below for the block is common to both.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE RIDGE IS THE ROUTE AND ITS HIGH POINT IS THE HANDOFF. Trail #601 runs along the crest to a high point near 5,920 ft, and everything after that is open ridge. In cloud you do not need a view: stay on the crest, going northeast, with the ground falling away on both sides. The moment you are sidehilling with the drop on only one side, you have come off the divide.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING, and this is the test that matters: the summit block of Hadley is a SHORT CLASS 3 STEP above loose scree, roughly the last 100 ft of the day. Everything below it is walking. So the base is the point where the ridge stops being walkable and stands up in a single short step. If you are scrambling for hundreds of feet you are on the wrong feature; if you have not scrambled at all you are not at the summit.

THE APPROACH IS NOT A LOOP AND CHOWDER RIDGE IS THE CONFIRMATION. You should arrive at the block having travelled along Chowder Ridge. If you are dropping into a basin or crossing a glacier to reach a rock block, you are somewhere else on the north side of Baker.

WHICH DIVIDE DID YOU WALK IN ON? This is the one thing to be sure of before you commit to a descent line in poor visibility, because the two approaches to this summit leave in different directions and neither is signed. Cougar Divide comes in from the NORTH-WEST via Dobbs Creek; Skyline Divide comes in from the WEST along a much longer open ridge. Note your entry point onto Chowder Ridge on the way up.
hazards: Eleven miles of rough gravel road, and a trailhead that mapping apps place short of the real one
Cross-country ridge travel with no tread and no cairns once past the 5,920 ft high point
Loose scree below a short Class 3 step
Open ridge with no shelter and no water beyond the trailhead
In cloud, two different divides converge on this summit and neither exit is marked

approach_variants.name: Skyline Divide Trail #678 and the long open ridge east to Chowder Ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Oct — but see the access note; this trailhead may not currently be reachable at all
approach_variants.notes:
ACCESS FIRST: from Glacier, WA drive SR-542 about a mile past the Glacier Public Service Center to Glacier Creek Road (FS-39), turn right, then immediately left onto Deadhorse Road (FS-37). FS-37 normally runs 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide trailhead. Under the Forest Service's current alert FS-37 is impassable at milepost 3.1 from 2021 flood damage with no estimated repair date, so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle. Confirm before planning around it.

When open, Skyline Divide Trail #678 climbs through old-growth switchbacks into meadows and reaches the ridge crest at about 4.4-4.5 miles. From there the route is cross-country along the open ridge — roughly three miles of it — to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley's summit block.

The first viewpoint on the crest near 6,600 ft is the landmark parties use to re-find the maintained trail on the way back.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 6,600 FT VIEWPOINT IS THE GATE, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. It is where maintained trail ends and where you rejoin it. In cloud it is the only reliable waypoint on this approach, because everything east of it is three miles of undifferentiated open ridge. Note it on the way out — parties who do not, spend the return walking a crest that all looks the same.

THE CREST IS THE HANDRAIL. From the viewpoint the route runs EAST along the ridge for roughly three miles to Chowder Ridge. Keep the crest under your feet with air on both sides; this ridge has heather benches falling away either side and it is easy to drift onto one and lose the line.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: the summit block is a SHORT CLASS 3 STEP above loose scree and talus — the last stretch of the day and the only scrambling on it. Walking stops, one short step of rock, summit. That is the whole climb, and it is the test: if you are scrambling for a long time, you are on a false feature; if you have not left your feet, you are not there.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH TO THIS SAME BLOCK: Cougar Divide arrives on Chowder Ridge from the NORTH-WEST after crossing near Dobbs Creek, and its trail high point is 5,920 ft. Skyline arrives from the WEST after roughly three miles of ridge from a 6,600 ft viewpoint. If you are descending in poor visibility, going down the wrong divide puts you 11 miles of gravel road away from your car on a road that may itself be washed out.
hazards: FS-37 impassable at milepost 3.1 with no repair date — the trailhead may not be drivable at all
Three miles of cross-country open ridge with no tread and no cairns
A short Class 3 step above loose scree and talus
Two unmarked divides converging on one summit, with very different roads at the bottom
No water once past the meadows

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 and the climbers' path past the pond to the toe of the Ruth Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE NAME CAREFULLY. This route is filed under a name that encodes the direction you WALK, not the side you climb: the line goes over Hannegan Pass and up the NORTH-side Ruth Glacier. Its aspect is N. A party expecting south-facing slopes will be looking for the wrong mountain-side all day.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FR-32, about 5.3 miles off SR-542, follow Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley. The first 2-2.5 miles climb gently through old growth with Ruth Creek alongside and views north to Mount Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge. Around mile 3, Hannegan Camp is a designated backcountry camp and the last reliably running water on the standard line; above it the trail switchbacks through meadows to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, about mile 4 and roughly 2,000 ft of gain.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail for a climbers' path heading east then south. Most parties camp on the far side of the notch northwest of Ruth's summit, on snow, to keep impact down.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE POND IS THE SINGLE HARDEST THING TO FIND AND THE ROUTE TURNS ON IT. At Hannegan Pass you leave maintained tread for a faint climbers' path that goes east then south, staying on the SOUTH SIDE OF A SMALL POND. The tread here is faint and partly hidden in trees, and this is the easiest place on the entire route to lose the line — flat light and early morning are when it happens. Find the pond, put it on your left, keep going south.

SECOND MARKER, AND IT IS TACTILE: after the pond the path goes up and LEFT AROUND THE BASE OF A CLIFF BAND onto a shoulder. A cliff band you have to walk around is a physical thing you cannot miss in cloud. If you are climbing straight up into rock, you have not gone far enough left.

ARRIVAL: from the shoulder, traverse SOUTH across heather and talus to gain the broad ridge feeding the toe of the Ruth Glacier's north slope at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. That is where you rope up, and it is the base of the climb. The transition is obvious underfoot — heather and talus give way to permanent snow.

TREAT IT AS A GLACIER FROM THE FIRST STEP, WHICH IS THE POINT THIS ENTRY MOST WANTS TO MAKE. The lower Ruth is a moderate, welcoming-looking snow slope and it looks like a walk. It has produced at least one documented crevasse fall in years with thin or soft cover. The pleasant appearance is exactly the hazard.

WHAT TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up and climber's-left brings you to the broad notch just northwest of Ruth's summit around 6,600 ft. That is the camp and the start of the traverse toward Icy Peak, not the base of this route.
hazards: A faint climbers' path at Hannegan Pass that parties routinely lose in flat light
A glacier that looks like a snow walk and has produced a crevasse fall
No reliable running water above Hannegan Camp in a typical snow year
Route-finding around a cliff band on a shoulder with no cairns
A long valley walk out after a summit day, commonly finished tired
