approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and Ruth Mountain first, then down to the Ruth-Icy saddle and across to the Icy Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Shares its trailhead and lower approach with the Ruth Glacier route: Trail #674 from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead up Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then the faint climbers' path east and south past the pond, around the cliff-band shoulder, and onto the Ruth Glacier's north slope to a camp near the notch northwest of Ruth's summit around 6,600 ft.

The traverse is conventionally done Ruth-to-Icy: tag Ruth's summit first, then descend roughly 800 ft south and west toward a gully on the peak's west side, pick up a faint boot path, and continue down another 800 ft or so — about 1,600 ft in total off Ruth's summit — to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft.

From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and follow talus and boot path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper.

The re-ascent of Ruth on the way home is the sting in the tail and cannot be avoided on the standard car-to-car version.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION THAT MATTERS IS WHICH LINE YOU TAKE OFF RUTH, AND IT IS NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE. There are two ways down the 1,600 ft to the Ruth-Icy saddle: a steeper, more direct gully that parties call the death gully, and cairned heather slopes and game trails to CLIMBER'S LEFT holding second and third class ground. Take the HEATHER, on the left. The direct gully is the one you will drift into if you simply point downhill, which is what makes this worth stating rather than assuming.

ARRIVAL AT THE SADDLE: it is the LOW POINT between the two peaks, around 6,600-6,800 ft, and there are trees in it. Trees are the confirmation — you have dropped below the alpine on both sides. If you are still on open snow or talus with nothing growing, you have not reached the saddle.

THE NOTCH WEST OF THE NORTHWEST SPIRE IS THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING, at about 6,500 ft. From the saddle, cross the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier and aim for a notch or saddle just WEST of Icy's Northwest Spire. Watch for a long horizontal crevasse near the top of the glacier below the Icy towers, and for a bergschrund near the notch in some seasons.

THE SUMMIT GULLY IS THE FINAL TEST AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS. From the notch, about 500 ft of second and third class up an obvious LEFT-HAND, LIGHT-COLOURED gully system reaches the base of the summit block. The climbing is a single 100 ft fourth-class gully with solid jugs and ledges, real exposure, and rappel slings around a horn at its top. Take the FIRST PROMINENT GULLY. Sling anchors at the top of a 100 ft gully are the arrival marker; if there is nothing at the top and the gully keeps going, you are in the wrong one.

AND THE ONE THAT CATCHES PEOPLE AT THE VERY END: the true high point is the SOUTHEAST point, about 11 ft higher than the peak most maps label as the top. The register is on the northwest summit. Decide before you leave the notch which one you are going to.
hazards: A steep loose 'death gully' that is the natural fall line off Ruth and the wrong line
A long horizontal crevasse near the top of the Icy Glacier below the towers
A bergschrund near the west notch in some seasons
Loose rock funnelled through a single summit gully with the whole party in it
Roughly 1,600-2,000 ft of re-ascent over Ruth on the way home, at the end of a twelve-hour day

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, over Ruth Mountain, then the Icy Glacier's northwest slope to the west notch
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at road's end on FS Road 32, near 3,100 ft, hike Trail #674 roughly four miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft. Hannegan Camp about 3.5 miles in is the LAST reliable water on the route — fill up there, because there is nothing running past it.

From the pass go cross-country east and northeast up heather meadows and scattered timber onto Ruth's north side, with some third-class ground through trees, then rope up for the Ruth Glacier to Ruth's summit at 7,115 ft. Most parties treat trailhead-to-camp as a five to six hour day and camp on Ruth's summit plateau or in the saddle beyond.

From camp, descend Ruth's south and west side about 800 ft to the Ruth-Icy saddle near 6,600 ft, taking the heather slopes and game trail on climber's LEFT rather than the steep loose gully. From the saddle, traverse talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the Icy Glacier.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ON THE ICY GLACIER, KEEP THE ROCK RIDGE ON YOUR LEFT AND THE CREVASSES ON YOUR RIGHT. That is the navigation instruction for the whole glacier and it works without seeing the summit: climb the northwest slope gradually southeast to about 6,500 ft with a rock ridge as your left-hand handrail. If the rock swings round to your right, you have crossed the glacier and are heading for the wrong side of the peak.

THE NOTCH IS THE BASE, AND IT IS WEST OF THE NORTHWEST SPIRE at roughly 6,500 ft. Traverse the upper glacier below Icy's west face, skirting the west notch — some seasons there is a bergschrund near the top of it — to reach the notch or saddle just west of the Northwest Spire.

THERE IS A LONG HORIZONTAL CREVASSE NEAR THE TOP OF THE GLACIER, right below the Icy towers, and it is a useful landmark rather than only a hazard: it runs across your line just where the glacier ends beneath the peak. Meeting it means you are at the top of the glacier.

THE CLIMBING STARTS AT THE FIRST PROMINENT GULLY. From the notch, about 500 ft of second and third class talus and snow up Icy's south side reaches the base of a LIGHT-COLOURED, roughly 100 FT FOURTH-CLASS GULLY on the LEFT, with solid jugs and ledges. There are rappel slings around a horn at its top, left by previous parties. Colour, length and the slings at the top are three independent confirmations, which is more than most gullies in the Cascades offer.

WHICH SUMMIT: the gully leads to the NORTHWEST summit, which holds the register. The true high point is a separate southeast tower about 11 ft higher, reached by more third and fourth class scrambling. Many parties only tag the northwest one — decide in advance rather than at the notch.

A FEW MOVES IN THE GULLY FEEL LOW FIFTH RATHER THAN FOURTH, depending on the exact line taken. That is not a sign you are off route; it is the route.
hazards: No water source at all after Hannegan Camp
Crevasses on both the Ruth and the Icy Glaciers, and a bergschrund near the west notch in some seasons
Loose rock in the summit gully with the whole party funnelled through it — helmets are standard
The steep loose 'death gully' off Ruth, which is the natural fall line and the wrong option
Roughly 2,000 ft of regain over Ruth on the way home

approach_variants.name: Ruth Creek crossing near milepost 3, then the Wall Street couloir to the Northwest Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep for the scramble; the couloir has also been climbed and skied in winter, when it is an avalanche path rather than a walk
approach_variants.notes:
Drive SR-542 to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to the pullout near milepost 3, just past where a creek flows over a concrete weir, at about 2,950 ft. This is NOT the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of the road.

Cross Ruth Creek. There is no bridge; parties cross on whatever logs are in place, and a three-log cluster has been used. Then about 45 minutes of thrashing through slide alder and devil's club to the avalanche debris at the foot of the snow gully.

The couloir runs roughly 1,500 vertical feet and opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft; from there the route crosses the glacier to a saddle near 6,500 ft and scrambles the southeast ridge to the summit.

Timing is the whole trade: earlier means more snow and more avalanche risk, later means thicker brush and discontinuous snow.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WALL STREET IS A CORRIDOR WITH WALLS ON BOTH SIDES, AND THAT IS THE TEST. Once you are in it, the gully holds a remarkably UNIFORM GRADIENT of 30-35 degrees and a UNIFORM WIDTH of about 50 feet, with very steep rock walls on BOTH sides, for roughly 1,500 vertical feet. Nothing else on this side of the valley does that. In cloud you do not need to see the top: if you can touch rock on your left and rock on your right and the angle is not changing, you are in Wall Street. If your gully fans out, or has a wall on only one side, it is not.

GETTING TO IT: the marker at the bottom is AVALANCHE DEBRIS. After the creek crossing and roughly 45 minutes of alder and devil's club, the brush ends at the debris pile at the foot of the snow gully. Debris is what tells you the gully above you actually runs — and it is also the reason to be there early and cold.

THE ARRIVAL AT THE TOP OF THE COULOIR IS THE GLACIER. The corridor opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft. Walls end, glacier starts.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER TWO ROUTES, and it is decided in the car park rather than on the mountain. THREE routes on Sefrit start from three different places: this one from the Ruth Creek pullout near MILEPOST 3 on Ruth Creek Road; the Bloody Head Couloir from the Ruth Creek TRAIL higher up the valley near 3,450 ft; and the Southwest Ridge from the NOOKSACK CIRQUE trailhead at the end of FR-34, a different road entirely. If you drove to the end of FR-34 you cannot reach this route today.
hazards: An unbridged crossing of Ruth Creek on logs that change year to year
45 minutes of slide alder and devil's club with no tread
A 1,500 ft avalanche path — the debris at its foot is the evidence
Crossing the Northwest Glacier above the couloir
Shattered summit rock on the southeast ridge

approach_variants.name: Leave the Ruth Creek trail near 3,450 ft, drop southwest across the creek and take talus to the couloir
approach_variants.season: Best when the couloir holds continuous snow. Parties have been turned around on wet, mossy, muddy rock in the lower couloir — this line wants snow cover, not bare rock
approach_variants.notes:
Same road access as the Southeast Ridge route: SR-542 to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) and Ruth Creek Road toward Hannegan Campground. This variant then goes further up the valley before leaving the trail.

From the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft, leave the trail, drop SOUTHWEST to cross Ruth Creek, and cross talus to the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft.

One documented attempt turned around near 4,300 ft on rock the party judged unmanageable — mossy, muddy and soaked. That is a real and repeatable outcome rather than an anomaly, and it is the main reason to want this line under snow.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS FOUND BY ELEVATION AND BEARING, NOT BY LOOKING FOR A FEATURE, AND THE TWO NUMBERS ARE 3,450 AND 4,000. You leave the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft and you meet the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft on the far side of the creek. Between them the instruction is a single word: SOUTHWEST. Drop to the creek, cross it, and go up the talus on the other side. Five hundred and fifty feet of gain from trail to base.

THE CONFIRMATION IS UNDERFOOT AND IT IS A WARNING AS WELL AS A MARKER. If the ground at 4,000 ft is bare, mossy, muddy and wet rather than snow, you have found the couloir in the condition that has already turned a party around. Being in the right place does not mean the route is in.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST WALL STREET, which is the same peak's other north-side gully and less than two miles away: Wall Street is entered from the pullout near MILEPOST 3 at about 2,950 ft, after a creek crossing and 45 minutes of alder, and it is a 50-ft-wide corridor with steep walls on both sides holding a uniform 30-35 degrees for 1,500 ft. Bloody Head is entered from the TRAIL at 3,450 ft, higher up the valley. If you walked up the valley on a trail before dropping to the creek, you are heading for Bloody Head. If you crossed the creek straight out of a pullout and thrashed alder, you are heading for Wall Street.

AND THE COARSE CHECK: both of these are on Sefrit's NORTH side and are reached from Ruth Creek. The Southwest Ridge is reached from the Nooksack Cirque trailhead on a different forest road and faces the other way.
hazards: An unbridged Ruth Creek crossing with no established log
A documented turnaround on wet, mossy, muddy rock in the lower couloir
Avalanche-prone gully terrain on Sefrit's north side
Loose rock and a shattered summit block on the peak generally
No maintained tread from the moment you leave the Ruth Creek trail

approach_variants.name: Nooksack Cirque Trailhead at the end of FR-34, then an ascending traverse through the cliff band
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Early summer high water can make the Ruth Creek ford at the trailhead difficult or unsafe
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, drive SR-542 east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR-34), and follow FR-34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead. This is a DIFFERENT trailhead from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR-32, and from the milepost-3 pullout the Wall Street route uses.

Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there is no bridge.

Follow the old roadbed and Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for roughly 50 minutes, then leave the trail and make an ascending traverse onto Sefrit's west and southwest ridge, passing through or around a cliff band, to reach the base of the summit gully system.

A separate, lower-angle line on the southeast side — Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier — is Class 2 with one exposed Class 3 traverse and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak. The two are easily confused in planning and impossible to confuse on the ground, because they start on different roads.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIFF BAND IS THE GATE, AND THE GULLY YOU WANT IS ABOVE IT. Fifty minutes up Trail #750 you leave the trail and traverse upward, passing through or around a cliff band. Everything below the band is approach; the summit gully system starts above it. If you are still under continuous rock, you have not got through the band yet.

THE GULLY SPLITS, AND THE ANSWER IS LEFTMOST. Above the cliff band the summit gully divides into several forks. Take the LEFTMOST fork — or, put the other way round, the one immediately WEST of a snow couloir lying to its right. Those two descriptions are the same instruction from two sides and together they are checkable in poor visibility: find the snow couloir, then take the rock fork on its left.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS A CONFIRMATION. On this line the rock is generally solid low down and gets looser near the summit ridge. If your fork is loose from the first moves, you are probably in one of the other forks.

WHICH SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN AM I ON? This is the coarse test and it is settled by the drive: this route starts on FR-34 at the NOOKSACK CIRQUE trailhead and works up the peak's WEST and SOUTHWEST side. Sefrit's other two routes are both reached from Ruth Creek on the NORTH side and neither of them can be reached from here without going back to the car.

DESCENT NOTE THAT CROSS-CHECKS THE START: parties reverse this line, and some rappel the short crux step off pre-existing slings rather than downclimb it. Slings on a short step above a cliff band is the same feature seen from above.
hazards: An unbridged ford of Ruth Creek at the trailhead, difficult or unsafe at early-summer high water
A cliff band to be negotiated on an unmarked ascending traverse
Several similar-looking forks in the summit gully, only one of which is the easy line
Loose rock near the summit ridge
Fixed slings of unknown age at the crux step

approach_variants.name: Goat Mountain Trail #673 to the end of maintained tread, then over the West Peak false summit
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow lingers on this ridge and reports have found solid snow from 4,300-4,500 ft well into summer
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goat Mountain Trailhead, day-use parking just off FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) about 2.1-2.5 miles up from the Glacier Public Service Center, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It is well built and relentlessly steep, gaining the ridge by dozens of switchbacks and crossing a small cascading creek repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock.

Around a mile in, near 3,200 ft, the grade eases and the trail traverses a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly two miles it crosses into the Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur — the Old Goat Trail — splits east toward an old lookout site. Stay on the main tread.

Meadows and big views open by 2.7 miles; the maintained trail tops out on the crest at a 5,200 ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft.

Beyond that it is an open ridge boot path, about 0.8 mile and 1,000 ft more to the West Peak false summit near 6,600 ft, and then on to the true East summit.

There is no reliable water beyond the creek crossings in the first mile.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL STOPS, NEAR 5,600 FT, AND THAT END IS ABRUPT. Below it, built tread and switchbacks. Above it, an open ridge boot path with nothing constructed. If you are still on graded trail you have not started the route.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS CORNICED — DO NOT GO OVER ITS TOP. This is the one hard rule on the ridge and it is a safety instruction rather than a route preference: the West Peak at about 6,600 ft is corniced and exposed, and the correct line bypasses it on the SOUTH or WEST slope. Cornices are invisible from above and this is precisely the terrain where cloud sits.

THE 300 FT DROP IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU HAVE PASSED THE FALSE SUMMIT, AND IT IS THE STRONGEST TEST ON THE ROUTE. Past the West Peak the ridge DROPS ROUGHLY 300 FT into a notch before climbing again. So: if you have not descended 300 ft, the high ground in front of you is not the true summit — it is the false one you were supposed to walk around. An altimeter settles this in zero visibility and eyesight does not.

AFTER THE NOTCH it is a final 1,400 ft of mixed snow, rock and short exposed steps to the true East summit at 6,892 ft. The crux is a narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top — keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow.

CARRY THE AXE FROM 4,300-4,500 FT, not from where the snow looks serious. That is where reports put the solid snow, and it is well below the point where a party without an axe realises it wanted one.
hazards: Cornices on the West Peak false summit, invisible from above
Solid lingering snow from 4,300-4,500 ft upward well into summer
A knife-edge-ish exposed section near the true summit
No reliable water beyond the first mile
An unsigned spur trail near the wilderness boundary that leads to an old lookout site instead

approach_variants.name: Goat Mountain Trail #673 to the viewpoint shoulder, then around the south side of the West Peak
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, but the traverse slopes hold snow and an axe is wanted early season
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and the same first four miles as the standard scramble: from Glacier, SR-542 east 12.5 miles to FR-32, then FR-32 to the Goat Mountain Trailhead near 2,470 ft, and Goat Mountain Trail #673 up the switchbacks and ridge to the viewpoint shoulder around 5,400-5,700 ft.

The difference is what you do with the West Peak. This line leaves the maintained trail at the shoulder and traverses BELOW the West Peak on its SOUTH side to gain the ridge running toward the East Peak, rather than going over the West Peak's corniced top.

It is the line that avoids the cornice problem, at the cost of a sidehill traverse on 40-50 degree slopes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAVERSE GOES UNDER THE WEST PEAK, NOT OVER IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING DECISION. From the viewpoint shoulder near 5,400-5,700 ft, leave the trail and traverse BELOW the West Peak on its SOUTH side. If you are gaining height toward a summit ahead of you, you are on the standard scramble over the false summit; if you are holding height and sidehilling with the peak above your left shoulder, you are on this one.

THE ANGLE IS THE CONFIRMATION. The traverse slopes run 40-50 degrees. That is steep enough that an axe and, early season, step-kicking or crampons are wanted, and it is steep enough to feel wrong if you have wandered onto easier ground. Easy walking on this traverse means you have dropped too low into the basin.

ARRIVAL: you have arrived at the climbing when the traverse delivers you onto the connecting RIDGE between the two peaks — ground with air on both sides, running east toward the higher summit. The scramble to the East Peak's top is the last short section above that ridge.

THE 300 FT REGAIN IS THE RETURN TEST, worth knowing before you commit: coming back, you descend to the saddle and then have to regain roughly 300 ft to reach the Goat Mountain Trail viewpoint shoulder. If you are heading home and only ever going downhill, you have missed the shoulder and are descending an unmaintained slope.

WHICH SUMMIT: the EAST peak is the true and higher one, near 6,890 ft. The West Peak at about 6,600 ft is the false summit that the standard route walks over the top of.
hazards: A sidehill traverse on 40-50 degree slopes, wanting an axe and sometimes crampons
Cornices on the West Peak above the traverse
A 300 ft regain on the return that is easy to walk past in cloud
No maintained tread from the viewpoint shoulder onward
No reliable water past the first mile of trail

approach_variants.name: Winchester Mountain Trail #685 from Twin Lakes to the 1935 lookout
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and the limiting factor is the last two miles of FS-3065 rather than the trail
approach_variants.notes:
From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft — the parking area between the two lakes, with a vault toilet — pick up Winchester Mountain Trail #685 heading north-northwest. It starts as a moderately steep, well-graded tread through blueberry and heather.

At roughly a quarter to half a mile there is a signed junction with High Pass Trail #676, which goes on toward the Gargett Mine and Mount Larrabee. Stay LEFT or straight to remain on #685.

Beyond the junction the trail leaves the last trees onto open, treeless southeast-facing slopes and climbs by tight switchbacks. Around 0.9 mile an unmarked climbers' path splits off offering a more direct, rougher scramble line up snow and scree; the standard trail continues by switchbacks and is the preferred line.

At about 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just west and south of the summit; a short final push along the open ridge reaches the 1935 fire lookout at 6,521 ft. About 3.4-3.5 miles round trip with 1,300 ft of gain.

There is no water on route or at the lookout.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THERE IS NO CLIMBING ON THIS ROUTE AND SAYING SO IS THE HONEST ANSWER — WHAT THERE IS, IS ONE JUNCTION YOU CAN GET WRONG AND ONE SLOPE THAT CAN HURT YOU. The route is a maintained trail from the car to the lookout, so 'the base' is the trailhead between the two lakes.

THE JUNCTION AT A QUARTER TO HALF A MILE IS THE ONLY REAL DECISION. #685 for Winchester goes LEFT or straight; #676 for High Pass, the Gargett Mine, Mount Larrabee, American Border Peak and the Pleiades goes RIGHT. It is signed, but it is the branch point for five different objectives in this basin and taking it by accident sends you toward a very much bigger day. If you find yourself contouring around the WEST side of Winchester Mountain and losing height toward a pass, you are on #676.

THE SECOND ONE IS UNMARKED, at about 0.9 mile: a climbers' path splits off up snow and scree as a direct alternative to the switchbacks. It is rougher and it is not the standard line. In cloud, a path that stops switchbacking and goes straight up is the wrong one.

ARRIVAL AT THE RIDGE: at roughly 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just WEST and SOUTH of the summit, with only a few hundred feet of open ridge left. Cresting a ridge with the lookout to your northeast is the confirmation.

THE REAL HAZARD IS THE UPPER SWITCHBACKS, and it is worth reading as a base finding of a different kind: steep snow lingers on the upper switchbacks and the southeast slopes into August in heavy-snow years, it hardens overnight, and the runout below is consequential. An ice axe is a reasonable thing to be carrying on a lookout trail in early season.
hazards: The last two miles of FS-3065, rough and one-lane in places, high-clearance recommended
Hard lingering snow on the upper switchbacks into August in heavy-snow years, over consequential runout
A signed junction at 0.25-0.5 mile that serves five much larger objectives
An unmarked climbers' path at 0.9 mile up snow and scree
No water on route or at the lookout

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes, High Pass Trail #676 over Low Pass, then the basin to the southwest spur
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep at best; snow lingers in the gully into August and in the avalanche chute below Winchester
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065; the last two miles are rough and many parties park lower and walk the road. From the trailhead follow Winchester Mountain Trail #685 briefly; at about half a mile a signed junction splits LEFT to the Winchester lookout and RIGHT onto High Pass Trail #676. Take the right fork.

#676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain, where steep exposed snowfields can linger into August, then goes over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is roughly two miles and an hour and a half to two hours from the trailhead. There is no reliable water past this point late season.

Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends. An unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100-200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face, passing a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at about 6,900 ft.

Keep the party to six or fewer and spread out. The rock here is notoriously loose even by Cascades standards.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO NARROW PARALLEL CHANNELS ABOUT THIRTY FEET APART. TAKE THE RIGHT-HAND ONE. That is the route-finding crux of the whole climb, it is at the southwest spur around 6,900 ft, and it is the sentence to have memorised before you leave camp. Both channels are cut into the same rock face, both look plausible, and only one of them opens into broken rock and gains the south ridge cleanly.

FINDING THE SPUR ITSELF, in order and without needing a view: leave the maintained trail at High Pass. Contour WEST on the climbers' path and lose 100-200 ft into the basin. Pass a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, and climb to about 6,900 ft. Losing height first is counterintuitive and correct; a party that only ever goes up from High Pass ends up on Larrabee's south arm ridge instead of in the basin under its face.

CONFIRM THE GULLY BY WHAT IT DOES: the right-hand channel NARROWS and then opens into broken rock that leads to the crest of the south ridge. A channel that stays uniform, or that cliffs out, is the other one.

ABOVE THE GULLY, FAVOUR THE WEST SIDE OF THE CREST. There is a faint boot path and scattered cairns, and both disappear for long stretches, so this is genuine route-finding rather than following.

WHAT THE NEIGHBOURING OBJECTIVE LOOKS LIKE: from the same High Pass the col in Larrabee's SOUTH ARM leads northeast to the Pleiades and the traverse under Larrabee's west flank leads to American Border Peak. Three separate objectives leave from one pass, so name yours before you set off.
hazards: Two nearly identical parallel gullies thirty feet apart, only one of which is the route
Notoriously loose and crumbly rock in the gully and on the upper ridge — helmets, small parties, spread out
An avalanche chute below Winchester Mountain holding steep snow into August
A faint boot path and cairns that disappear for long sections above the gully
No reliable water past High Pass late season

approach_variants.name: High Pass and the Gargett Mine, then the long sidehill under Larrabee to the South AmBo Saddle
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and never on wet grass or wet rock
approach_variants.notes:
CONTAMINATION WARNING BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: this is AMERICAN Border Peak, 7,998 ft, in Washington. CANADIAN Border Peak is about a kilometre north across the international line and is a different mountain with its own routes, reached from British Columbia. Beta for the two is routinely mixed up because both are called 'Border Peak'. Everything here is the Washington approach from Twin Lakes.

From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft, take the High Pass Trail; at a quarter mile it splits from the short spur up Winchester Mountain — stay LEFT, north. The trail contours the west side of Winchester, dips across Low Pass, and climbs to High Pass near 5,960 ft, about two miles and 750 ft of gain, where Mount Baker comes into view south.

At High Pass leave the maintained tread and follow the climbers' path east and northeast DOWN to the old Gargett Mine workings around 5,400 ft. The mine creek is the last reliable water until lingering snow high on the peak.

From the mine, traverse north and contour onto Mount Larrabee's southwest and west flanks. This is a long, unmarked, exposed sidehill of well over a mile across steep talus, scree, heather and brush.

Most parties camp at Gargett Basin or in the moraine bowl and climb from there rather than pushing summit day from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 6,200-6,300 FT NOTCH ON LARRABEE'S NORTHWEST RIB IS THE FIRST GATE, AND THE SOUTH AMBO SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,840 FT IS THE SECOND. Those two are the whole navigation of this approach and both are cols — places where the ridge is low and you can stand on the crest with ground falling away on the far side. In cloud you are counting cols, not looking at the peak.

BETWEEN THEM IS A RED TALUS AND MORAINE BOWL. From the notch you drop slightly into it and then climb north out of it, up and across a series of steep gullies and ribs, to the saddle. Red rock underfoot after the first col is the confirmation you are in the right bowl.

ARRIVAL AT THE SADDLE: it is on the ridge crest DIRECTLY SOUTH of the summit. Standing there, the peak is north of you and Larrabee is behind you to the south. That bearing is the check — this is not a saddle you reach with the mountain to one side.

WHERE THE CLIMBING ACTUALLY STARTS IS 200 YARDS ABOVE THE SADDLE, NOT AT IT. From the saddle, go up the ridge crest on a faint climbers' path for roughly 200 yards, THEN start traversing RIGHTWARD on slabby RED LEDGES. The rock scrambling begins where the angle steepens noticeably at a distinctive rock rib: the first real move is up a small Class 3.5 cleft CLOSELY LEFT OF THAT RIB.

DE GAULLE'S NOSE IS THE AIMING MARK ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE RED FACE, at about 7,300 ft. The rising traverse across the red slopes goes toward it and the crossing feels very exposed. Beyond it come two 60-metre gullies with a sand-covered ledge traverse between them, and a chimney at the top of the second reached by a very airy ledge. If your route has no red traverse and no pair of long gullies, it is not this one.

AND THE HARD CONDITION RULE: do not attempt the Larrabee sidehill on wet grass or wet rock. Multiple accounts flag that as a genuine no-go rather than a discomfort.
hazards: Chronic rockfall — the defining hazard of this approach, helmets on from the Larrabee traverse
A long unmarked exposed sidehill on steep talus, scree, heather and brush
Wet grass or wet rock on the sidehill is a documented no-go condition
Two 60 m gullies of loose rock with climber-triggered rockfall onto the party below
Two to four rappels on descent off aged natural tat, with at least one recorded stuck and abandoned rope

approach_variants.name: Yellow Aster Butte Trail #686 over Gold Run Pass, then the Tomyhoi Arm ridge to the moat below the false summit
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. The moat below the false summit opens as the season goes on and is the crux either way
approach_variants.notes:
From the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead — also called the Keep Kool trailhead, around 3,600-3,700 ft — on Twin Lakes Road (FR-3065), start on Yellow Aster Butte Trail #686. It climbs through forest switchbacks with a couple of seasonal creek crossings in the first mile.

At roughly 2.3-2.5 miles near 5,400 ft the signed Tomyhoi Lake Trail splits off RIGHT. Stay left and continue toward Gold Run Pass near 5,900 ft, then contour into the Yellow Aster Meadows and a basin of small tarns at about 5,200-5,600 ft — roughly two hours and four miles from the car, and the last dependable water.

From the basin leave maintained trail: head north-northwest over a broad hump and down to a col around 6,266 ft, then pick up a well-defined boot-packed climbers' path along the crest of the Tomyhoi Arm.

As the ridge narrows above roughly 6,800-7,000 ft, bypass the narrowest sections on broad benches on the NORTH — right — side rather than staying on the crest. The path fades into scree and talus near the toe of the Tomyhoi Glacier.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A MOAT, NOT A LEDGE — THE CLIMBING STARTS WHERE THE GLACIER MEETS THE ROCK AT ABOUT 7,200-7,250 FT, AT A NOTCH IN THE JAGGED RIDGE BELOW THE FALSE SUMMIT. Traverse along the TOP EDGE of the Tomyhoi Glacier to avoid several rock pinnacles, and aim for that notch. Getting into it means a traverse on hard snow around a small moat, and in many years that shallow rock-and-ice moat is the crux of the entire outing.

THE ROCK BY THE GLACIER IS GLACIER-POLISHED AND SLICK, and that is a tactile confirmation you are in the right place as well as a warning. Smooth, scoured rock at the snow margin means you are at the moat.

THERE IS A DOCUMENTED ALTERNATIVE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: drop 100 to 200 ft LOWER and climb a rock finger to reach the same notch. A party that arrives at an open moat it does not like has a published option other than retreat.

GEAR IS GENUINELY DISPUTED HERE and the honest statement is that reports differ: some parties manage the moat traverse with an ice axe alone on firm snow, others want crampons. It opens as the season goes on. Carry for the worse case.

ABOVE THE NOTCH, THE SEQUENCE IS THE CHECK: an exposed traverse around a rib gains the climbable side of the summit block, then roughly 160 ft along the LEFT edge of the ridge, then a ledge crossed WEST to a wide corner where the crux is a short V-shaped SLOT. Third class throughout with that one slot harder. The block looks far worse from the false summit than it climbs — repeatedly, in every account — so an intimidating view from the false summit is not evidence you are off route.

OLD RING PITONS ON THE ROUTE are a reminder this is not a maintained line, not a sign you are on the right one.
hazards: A rock-and-ice moat at the notch that is the crux of the outing and widens through the season
Glacier-polished slick rock at the snow margin
Minor crevasse hazard traversing the top edge of the Tomyhoi Glacier
Loose, exposed, non-obvious route-finding on scree and rock benches approaching the notch
The descent through the V-slot is the most exposed step of the day and is where parties rope up

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes and High Pass, then the col in Larrabee's south arm and the gully to the notch
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, WA, drive SR-542 east about 12 miles to the WSDOT Shuksan maintenance facility and turn onto Twin Lakes Road (FS-3065). The first 4.5 miles to the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead are passenger-car friendly; beyond that the road narrows and is not maintained for passenger vehicles, and high-clearance is recommended for the final two miles to Twin Lakes. If the upper road is out, park at the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and add roughly four miles round trip and 1,500 ft of gain.

From the isthmus between the Twin Lakes take the High Pass Trail — about two miles, LOSING roughly 300 ft as it skirts below Winchester Mountain before climbing to the pass.

From High Pass, ascend the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's SOUTH ARM; there is a trail here in summer. From the col descend slightly and traverse the basin.

The Pleiades are a series of jagged spires on Larrabee's east ridge, so this is not one summit but several.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIMB STARTS AT A GULLY LEADING TO THE NOTCH BETWEEN THE FIRST AND SECOND PLEIADES, AND FINDING IT IS A THREE-STEP SEQUENCE FROM HIGH PASS. Up the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's south arm. DOWN slightly from the col. ACROSS the basin. Then UP the gully to the notch. The descent in the middle is the step people skip, and skipping it puts you on Larrabee's south ridge instead.

THE NOTCH IS BETWEEN TWO SPIRES AND THAT IS THE CONFIRMATION. You are not aiming for a summit, you are aiming for the gap between the first and second towers of a jagged row. Arriving somewhere with rock on both sides of you and the basin below is the arrival.

FROM THE NOTCH THE TWO PEAKS ARE VERY DIFFERENT, AND THE CHOICE MATTERS. The SECOND peak, to the EAST, is an easy scramble. The FIRST peak, to the WEST, is third class in summer and has been reported as a snowy knife-edge with slabby, high-consequence exposure in winter conditions. Going the wrong way out of the notch is the difference between a walk and a serious ridge.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG OBJECTIVE LOOKS LIKE: Larrabee's own South Ridge route leaves the same basin and its base is TWO PARALLEL CHANNELS about 30 ft apart on a southwest spur at 6,900 ft — take the right-hand one for Larrabee. American Border Peak's route contours much further north around Larrabee's west flank to a col at 6,200-6,300 ft. All three leave High Pass. Only this one crosses the basin under Larrabee's EAST-side spires.

THE ROCK IS LOOSE AND SANDY throughout, which makes downclimbing as hazardous as the climb up. Keep the party close so nobody is under a falling stone.
hazards: Loose sandy rock where downclimbing is as hazardous as ascending
A rough final two miles of FS-3065 that may add four miles and 1,500 ft to the day
Three separate objectives leaving from High Pass, easy to confuse in the basin
The first (west) Pleiad is far more serious than the second and looks similar from the notch
No water past High Pass

approach_variants.name: Bagley Lakes and Chain Lakes Trail to the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then cross-country to the ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow lingers on the slope below Herman Saddle into July or August and the Forest Service flags it as avalanche terrain in winter and spring
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Bagley Lakes Trailhead around 4,200 ft, at the south end of the upper Mount Baker Ski Area parking lot near the Heather Meadows Visitor Center. Follow Bagley Lakes Trail #684.1 south along the east shore of Bagley Lake — the only reliable water on the route, and it should still be treated.

At about three quarters of a mile the trail joins Chain Lakes Trail #682, which bends east and switchbacks up toward Herman Saddle at roughly 5,300 ft, about 1.5-2 miles and 1,100 ft above the lakes.

At the last switchback BELOW Herman Saddle, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather and a short band of scrub trees for a couple of hundred vertical feet to gain the connecting ridge between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman.

Then follow the crest generally EAST, staying mostly on the south and southwest side over heather benches and loose scree and talus, to the base of a short final east ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE EXIT IS BELOW THE SADDLE, NOT AT IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM. You leave Chain Lakes Trail #682 at the LAST SWITCHBACK BELOW Herman Saddle. The correct exit point is easy to miss in poor visibility and this is the route-finding crux of the day.

SO USE THE SADDLE AS A BACKSTOP RATHER THAN A TARGET. Herman Saddle is the LOW POINT on the ridge connecting Mazama Dome, to the west, and Mount Herman, to the east. If you crest the saddle and the ground starts falling away in front of you toward the Chain Lakes basin, you have gone past your exit — turn round and come back down to the last switchback. That is a reliable test in cloud precisely because a saddle announces itself underfoot.

WHAT YOU CLIMB TO REACH THE RIDGE: open heather slopes and a short band of SCRUB TREES, a couple of hundred vertical feet. Scrub trees at the top of a heather slope is the marker; if you are on scree with nothing growing, you are too high or too far east.

ARRIVAL: you are on the route when you are standing on the Mazama Dome-Herman connecting ridge with a peak at each end of it. From there the direction is EAST, on the south and southwest side of the crest.

THE CLIMBING ITSELF IS THE LAST SHORT EAST RIDGE. Everything before it is heather benches, loose scree and talus. If you have not left your feet by the time the ground runs out ahead of you, you are not at the summit yet; the true top takes a short scramble up that final ridge.

WHICH BUMP IS MAZAMA DOME? It is the WEST end of the same ridge. Turning west out of the saddle area climbs a different, lower feature.
hazards: An unmarked exit at the last switchback below the saddle, easy to miss in poor visibility
Lingering snow on the Chain Lakes switchbacks into July or August, flagged as avalanche terrain in winter and spring
Loose down-sloping scree and talus on the connecting ridge, easy to kick onto anyone below
Only one water source, at Bagley Lake, and it needs treating
Two summits on one ridge — Mazama Dome west, Herman east

approach_variants.name: Table Mountain Trail #681 from the Artist Point lot, up the southeast-face switchbacks
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it is the road and the snow in the cliff band that decide it rather than the calendar
approach_variants.notes:
From the Artist Point trailhead at about 5,100 ft, at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, walk to the NORTHWEST CORNER of the large paved parking lot. Table Mountain Trail #681 starts OPPOSITE THE VAULT TOILETS, on the side of the lot away from the highway.

The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path and reaches its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there it climbs a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — a narrow, exposed catwalk with drops of 400-800 ft toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek.

After roughly 400 ft of gain, about 0.4-0.5 mile from the car, the switchbacks top out on the broad flat summit plateau. Follow the tread west-northwest along the south rim; braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.3 miles two small tarns frame Mount Shuksan and mark the usual high point.

There is no water: the tarns are shallow and silty. Carry everything from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ONE THING PEOPLE GET WRONG HERE IS THE TRAILHEAD, AND IT IS IN A CAR PARK. The Artist Point lot is large and paved and has several trails leaving it. Table Mountain Trail #681 starts at the NORTHWEST CORNER, OPPOSITE THE VAULT TOILETS, on the side AWAY from the highway. Three independent descriptors for one gate — corner, toilets, away from the road — which is what you want when the lot is in cloud.

THE CLIMBING, SUCH AS IT IS, STARTS AT THE FIRST SWITCHBACK, a few hundred feet in. From there the route is a catwalk cut into the cliff band, and the tread is loose rock and gravel over hard pack with a 400-800 ft drop on the outside.

THE CLIFF BAND IS THE CRUX AND ALSO THE TURNAROUND POINT FOR MOST EARLY-SEASON PARTIES. Snow or verglas lingers in this section into July, and many parties turn back here without traction devices. That is the honest statement of what this route is: 400 ft of exposed switchback, then a walk.

ARRIVAL ON THE TABLE: after roughly 400 ft of gain the switchbacks top out on a broad, relatively flat plateau. Flat ground is the confirmation you are through the cliff band.

ON THE PLATEAU, HUG THE SOUTH RIM. Numerous braided use-trails cross the tabletop, and in cloud a plateau with braided paths is the easiest place on this route to end up walking in the wrong direction. The south rim looks straight down onto the Chain Lakes Trail and is the handrail.

WHERE TO STOP: the two small tarns at about 1.3 miles are the last easily identified landmark. Beyond them the trail degrades into an unmaintained scramble path descending toward the Table Mountain Glacier. If the path starts going DOWN and gets rough, you have passed the point most parties turn around at.
hazards: An exposed catwalk cut into a cliff band with 400-800 ft drops and loose gravel underfoot
Snow or verglas in the cliff band into July, which is the usual reason parties turn back
Braided use-trails on a flat plateau, the classic place to lose direction in cloud
No water — the summit tarns are shallow and silty
Beyond the tarns the tread degrades into an unmaintained scramble toward the glacier

approach_variants.name: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the 4,900 ft saddle, then the boot path and cairns over Peak 5681
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep snow-free; winter and spring ascents are done by experienced parties with mountaineering gear on a stable snowpack
approach_variants.notes:
From the Austin Pass / Artist Point trailhead at the end of SR-542, follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600. It DROPS about 700 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up past Lake Ann — 4.1 miles one way to the lake area — to a saddle at 4,900 ft northwest of the lake.

From the saddle, leave the maintained trail for a boot path heading southwest then south along the ridge crest. Where the ridge steepens near 5,300 ft the path contours the EAST side before the crest re-forms; from there follow cairns over Peak 5681 and scramble roughly half a mile west along the summit ridge to Mount Ann.

About 10.5 miles round trip with roughly 4,000 ft of cumulative gain, most of which comes from the fact that the trail loses 700 ft at the start and you pay it back at the end.

NOTE ON THE NAME: this is the Lake Ann below Artist Point on SR-542, not the Lake Ann near Maple Pass. This catalog has already had one route carrying the wrong Lake Ann's trailhead.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 4,900 FT SADDLE NORTHWEST OF THE LAKE IS WHERE THE ROUTE STARTS, AND IT IS THE LAST PIECE OF MAINTAINED TRAIL. Below it, built tread. Above it, a boot path. If you are still on graded trail heading toward the Fisher Chimneys and Shuksan, you have walked past your turn — that is the same trail, continuing.

THE BEARING OUT OF THE SADDLE IS SOUTHWEST, THEN SOUTH, ALONG THE CREST. Two headings in sequence. In cloud, keep the crest under your feet.

THE ONE PLACE THE ROUTE LEAVES THE CREST IS NEAR 5,300 FT, AND IT GOES EAST. Where the ridge steepens the path contours the EAST side before the crest re-forms above. Contouring west here puts you on the wrong side of the ridge above the Swift Creek basin.

CAIRNS ARE THE HANDRAIL ABOVE 5,300 FT, and losing them is the main route-finding hazard in poor visibility, in both directions. Note them going up.

ARRIVAL: the scrambling ridge runs roughly half a mile WEST from Peak 5681 to Mount Ann's summit. Peak 5681 is not the top — if you are standing on a high point and there is more ridge running west, keep going.

AND THE RETURN TRAP, which is worth stating because it is a cliff problem rather than a navigation one: coming back, stay HIGH on the ridge rather than contouring low where the path is indistinct. Contouring low here cliffs out above the basin.
hazards: Cairns as the only navigation above 5,300 ft, in both directions
Contouring low on the return, which cliffs out above the Swift Creek basin
A 700 ft descent at the start that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
Two Lake Anns in the North Cascades, one of which has already misplaced a trailhead in this catalog
Lingering snow on the traverse in early season

approach_variants.name: FS-3160 road-end boot path to Church Lake, then the basin rim to the 6,066 ft saddle
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow patches persist into July on shaded ground and in the summit gullies
approach_variants.notes:
From the FS-3160 road-end parking, reached via Canyon Creek Road (FS-31) then FS-3160, the route follows an unmaintained but heavily used boot path — not a numbered Forest Service trail. It climbs steeply through forest for about 0.6-0.7 mile and roughly 400 ft to Church Lake, a small emerald subalpine lake in a cirque directly below Bearpaw's north side. This first stretch is the steepest sustained grade of the day.

Skirt the lake along its east (left) shore; the best flat campsites are on the far side.

Beyond the lake the tread fades into intermittent boot path and cairns through meadows and heather benches. Keep LEFT — west — up the basin rim toward a broad saddle around 6,066 ft on the ridge separating Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block. That stretch accounts for most of the remaining 900 ft of the route's 1,300 ft total gain over roughly 1.5 miles one way.

Church Lake is the last reliable water.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CHURCH LAKE IS THE HANDRAIL AND IT IS UNMISSABLE — 0.6 TO 0.7 MILE UP, 400 FT OF GAIN, AND THE STEEPEST GROUND OF THE DAY IS BEHIND YOU WHEN YOU REACH IT. Everything about this route is oriented from the lake. Skirt it on its EAST, left-hand, shore.

ABOVE THE LAKE THE INSTRUCTION IS ONE WORD: LEFT. Keep left — west — up the basin rim. The tread is intermittent boot path and cairns through meadows and heather benches and there is nothing built to follow, so the bearing is what you navigate on.

THE 6,066 FT SADDLE IS THE TOP OF THE APPROACH, AND IT IS A COL: a broad low point on the ridge separating the Church Lake basin from the summit block, with ground falling away on the far side. Arriving somewhere you can see down both sides is the confirmation.

FROM THE SADDLE, DROP SLIGHTLY AND TRAVERSE NORTH. The base of the summit block is across a rocky heather bowl to the north. That short descent is the step people skip; a party that keeps climbing straight off the saddle is on the ridge rather than under the block.

THE CLIMBING IS THE LAST 300 FT AND NOTHING BELOW IT. From the base of the block, roughly 300 ft of easy Class 2-3 on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure only in the last stretch, reaches the 6,091 ft summit. If you are scrambling for much more than 300 ft you are on the wrong feature.

DESCENT SHORTCUT WORTH KNOWING, because it changes what you should look for on the way up: many parties come down a scree and dirt chute that cuts straight from the ridge to the lake shore, shortcutting the traverse. It is loose. Noting where it tops out on the way up is what makes it usable on the way down.
hazards: An unmaintained boot path with no numbered trail and no maintained tread past the lake
Intermittent cairns through meadows and heather with nothing built to follow
Snow patches into July on shaded ground and in the summit gullies
A loose scree and dirt descent chute that parties use as a shortcut
Church Lake is the last water

approach_variants.name: Clearwater Creek gate, the logging roads to the cairn at mile 5, then the clearcut spur to the west ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the scramble. In May and June parties still get up it but the north-slope snowfield is in play
approach_variants.notes:
This is a Twin Sisters approach, so start with the range check: the Twin Sisters here are the olivine peaks west of Mount Baker, reached off Mosquito Lake Road and the Middle Fork Nooksack. Every road name below belongs to that range and to no other Twin Sisters.

Drive to the gate before the Clearwater Creek / Middle Fork Nooksack crossing on the logging-road network west of Mosquito Lake Road. From the gate it is roughly 6-6.5 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car to summit, almost all of it on old logging road and then ridge — one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble, and most parties mountain-bike the road.

Cross the bridge over Clearwater Creek and climb the well-graded logging road about 2.5 miles. At the first major fork stay RIGHT; the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry. About 0.2 mile later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the LEFT branch.

Around mile 5 the road walking ends. From there an old overgrown spur switchbacks up through a clearcut, and by about mile 6.4 you pass an old fire ring and enter a final band of brush before timber at the base of the west ridge.

The roads are on private timberland; access status changes, so confirm before the trip.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRT MOUND AND CAIRN AT ABOUT MILE 5 IS THE MOST IMPORTANT MARKER ON THIS APPROACH, BECAUSE IT IS WHERE THE NAVIGATION GETS HARD. Up to there you are on graded logging road and the only decisions are two forks — RIGHT at the first major fork about 2.5 miles in, then LEFT at the next fork 0.2 mile past the second bridge. At the mound and cairn near mile 5, leave the road for an old overgrown spur that switchbacks up through the clearcut.

THE FIRE RING AT ABOUT MILE 6.4 IS THE SECOND MARKER, and it confirms you took the right spur. Past it is a final band of brush and then timber at the base of the west ridge.

IN LOW CLOUD, WHICH IS NORMAL HERE, THE CLEARCUT IS THE HARDEST GROUND ON THE ROUTE AND IT IS NOT THE MOUNTAIN. There are no cairns and no defined tread through the clearcut and lower ridge, and the terrain is genuinely featureless. Parties should be prepared to navigate this section by map and GPS. The brush will also soak you to the waist without any rain falling.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: follow the timbered ridge up until it opens onto rock. Trees stop, rock starts, Class 3 begins. There is no bergschrund, no notch and no col to look for — the transition is vegetative.

THE ONE PIECE OF BETA THAT REPEATS IN EVERY ACCOUNT, AND IT IS THE FOG TEST FOR THE RIDGE ITSELF: STAY LEFT — CLIMBER'S LEFT — ON THE CREST. Cairns mark a Class 3 line that way. Drifting RIGHT leads to false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 ground on loose, exposed rock. If the climbing has got harder than Class 3 and the rock has got worse, you have drifted right; traverse back left rather than pushing on.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS A CONFIRMATION YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT RANGE. The Twin Sisters are dunite — olivine-rich ultramafic rock, exceptionally grippy, commonly compared to coarse sandpaper. If the rock under your hands is ordinary Cascade granite or volcanic rubble, you are not on the Sisters.
hazards: Route-finding through a featureless clearcut with no cairns and no tread, in the cloud that is normal here
Brush that saturates clothing and boots without rain
Drifting right on the crest into unintended Class 4-5 on loose, exposed rock
Private timberland access that changes year to year
No water after Clearwater Creek near the gate

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate at the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, then the Dailey Prairie roads to the West Ridge path
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The other documented way onto the same ridge, from the other side of the road network: via Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38. Park at the gate near 1,200 ft and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads — commonly by mountain bike — to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.

Several forks and offshoots near Dailey Prairie make GPS or a GPX track genuinely useful here; wrong turns on this network are common and expensive.

The gate situation on this network changes year to year. Treat the drivable road-end as unverified until confirmed for your trip.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROAD NETWORK IS THE CRUX AND THE MOUNTAIN IS NOT. Around Dailey Prairie the logging roads fork repeatedly with no signage, every branch looks like the main line, and a wrong turn costs miles. Carry a track. This is the one approach in this batch where the recommendation to navigate electronically is in the source material rather than an editorial addition.

THE END OF RIDEABLE ROAD IS THE MARKER, and on this network it is commonly identified by a LARGE CULVERT PIPE at the timber-road terminus. Stash bikes there and continue on foot.

THE CLIMBERS' PATH IS BRUSHY AND WET AND NOT HARD TO FOLLOW — that combination is itself the confirmation. It climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.

ARRIVAL: the same as the other variant, because it is the same ridge. Timber gives way to rock and Class 3 scrambling starts. On the crest, STAY CLIMBER'S LEFT; drifting right puts you on false summits and unintended Class 4-5 ground.

WHICH SISTER AM I ON? This matters because the same road network serves North Twin, South Twin, Little Sister, Cinderella and Skookum, and the peaks look alike. NORTH TWIN's west ridge tops out at 6,644 ft and is reached from the road network north of the range. SOUTH TWIN's west ridge is gained at an obvious NOTCH in the ridge crest around 5,200 ft above Orsino Creek Basin, and its summit is 7,004 ft. If your ridge started at a defined notch, you are on South Twin.
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network around Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
Private-timberland gates whose status changes year to year
The same drift-right-into-Class-5 trap on the ridge crest
Brushy, wet climbers' path with no maintained tread
Long approach with no water above the road network

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate, bike the Dailey Prairie roads, then Orsino Creek Basin to the 5,200 ft notch
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Oct, with snow-free scrambling typically Jul-Sep. Earlier or later trips want an ice axe for lingering snow near 6,500 ft
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River near 1,200 ft at the end of FR-38, reached via Mosquito Lake Road off WA-542. From the gate most parties mountain-bike the old quarry and logging road system for roughly 6-6.5 miles and 800-1,000 ft of gain, threading several forks near Dailey Prairie, until the road becomes too rough or overgrown to ride — usually marked by a large culvert pipe at the timber-road terminus. GPS or a GPX track is genuinely recommended on this network.

Stash bikes and pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot: brushy, wet, occasionally overgrown, but not hard to follow. It drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and fades out at a red talus slope which often holds snow well into summer.

From the talus, traverse RIGHTWARD — south — up and across, over a timbered rib, past the ruins of an old miner's log cabin, then up into Orsino Creek Basin. Orsino Creek is the last reliable water before the climb.

About four miles of foot travel from the bike cache to the ridge, four to five hours one way for most parties, with combined bike and foot gain around 4,600 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE RUINS OF AN OLD LOG CABIN ARE THE ONE MAN-MADE THING ON THIS APPROACH AND THEY ARE THE CHECKPOINT. From the red talus slope where the climbers' path fades, traverse RIGHT — south — up and across, cross a timbered rib, and pass the cabin ruins. If you have not passed a collapsed cabin, you have not made the traverse and you are still below the basin.

ORSINO CREEK IS THE LAST WATER AND THE ENTRY TO THE BASIN. Fill up. There is nothing above it.

THE BASE IS AN OBVIOUS NOTCH IN THE RIDGE CREST AT ABOUT 5,200 FT, AND YOU GET TO IT UP A STEEP LOOSE DIRT GULLY. That combination — an unpleasant slog up steep dirt, scree and talus, then a defined notch in a crest — is the arrival, and it works in cloud because a notch is a thing you stand in with air on the far side. This is the standard start and it is where the West Ridge is gained down low.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTE OUT OF THIS BASIN, AND IT IS A SINGLE NUMBER: the NORTH RIDGE route continues HIGHER and further CLIMBER'S LEFT — north — up basin snow or talus to a saddle around 5,800 ft between North Twin's southeast ridge and South Twin's north ridge. So 5,200 ft and the obvious notch is the West Ridge; 5,800 ft and a saddle between two peaks is the North Ridge. Six hundred feet and a bearing separate two routes that share every step of the approach up to the basin.

THE ROCK CONFIRMS THE RANGE: dunite, olivine-rich, exceptionally grippy, like coarse sandpaper. It is why parties choose to gain the ridge low rather than high — to maximise time on it.

HIGHER UP, THE FALSE-SUMMIT BYPASS IS WORTH CARRYING BEFORE YOU NEED IT: about 200 yards short of the false summit, leave the crest to the RIGHT — south — traverse ledges, and regain the crest roughly 500 ft lower. Staying exactly on the crest through that step is what forces parties into an improvised rappel.
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network near Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
A red talus slope holding snow into summer, and lingering snow near 6,500 ft
A steep loose dirt gully to gain the notch
Low fifth-class steps on the upper crest that force an improvised rappel if the bypass is missed
Orsino Creek is the last water for the whole climb

approach_variants.name: Dailey Prairie roads and Orsino Creek Basin, then higher and left to the 5,800 ft saddle
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Earlier gives firmer snow bridges on the Sisters Glacier and more crevasse-fall risk; later opens the crevasses and widens the moat
approach_variants.notes:
Access is via the Dailey Prairie logging-road network from the Middle Fork Nooksack River bridge near 1,200 ft on the north side of the range. The DNR and private gate situation changes year to year, so treat the drive-in as unverified until confirmed.

From wherever the gate stops you, most parties bike roughly 6-7 miles of climbing and quarry road, stashing bikes near the old pipe barrier at the end of road, at the base of the western cirque between North Twin and South Twin.

From there a climbers' path — brushy, overgrown and wet but not hard to follow — drops into timber and works southeast, fading into a red talus slope. Traverse RIGHT, south, across the talus, cross a timbered rib, and pass the ruins of an old log cabin. Orsino Creek along this stretch is the last reliable water for the climb and the camp.

Beyond the creek the path becomes a steep grind of dirt, scree and talus into the open basin below the North Twin / South Twin cirque, often holding snow into midsummer.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A SADDLE BETWEEN TWO PEAKS AT ABOUT 5,800 FT, AND THE MISTAKE THAT COSTS YOU THE ROUTE IS STOPPING SIX HUNDRED FEET LOWER. This approach is identical to the West Ridge's as far as Orsino Creek Basin. The West Ridge gains the crest at an OBVIOUS NOTCH around 5,200 ft. This route deliberately does not: it continues HIGHER and further CLIMBER'S LEFT — north — up basin snow or talus to the saddle between NORTH TWIN's southeast ridge and SOUTH TWIN's north ridge.

SO THE TEST IS: CAN YOU SEE, OR FEEL, GROUND RISING ON BOTH SIDES OF YOU TO TWO SEPARATE PEAKS? A notch in one ridge is the West Ridge. A col with a mountain at each end is the North Ridge. That distinction survives cloud because it is about the shape of the ground you are standing on.

EXPECT THE ROUTE-FINDING TO BE THE CRUX OF THE APPROACH RATHER THAN OF THE CLIMB. Multiple plausible lines run up the basin headwall depending on snow coverage, and parties consistently report the basin slog and the final gain to the notch as the most tedious and least obvious part of the day.

ABOVE THE SADDLE THE FIRST GROUND IS GLACIER, NOT ROCK. The crest is gained by way of the Sisters Glacier and the snow on the north side of the ridge. In early summer coverage is good and bridges are reported solid, but treat it as glacier travel. THE MOAT WHERE SNOW MEETS ROCK IS THE RECURRING OBSTACLE and it widens through the season — late in the year parties are stopped by the moat rather than by the crevasses.

THE HIGH NOTCH AT ROUGHLY 6,600 FT IS THE DECISION POINT ON THE ROUTE, not the base. Above it the character changes, and it is where you choose between the steep exposed final crest and the south-side gully bypass. If you have reached a distinct notch at 6,600 ft you are 800 ft above the start of the climbing.

AND THE DOCUMENTED ROUTE-FINDING TRAP IS NEAR THE TOP: parties that drift too high and too far RIGHT below the summit get cliffed out and have had to rappel to get back on line.
hazards: Glacier travel on the Sisters Glacier with a moat at the rock margin that widens all season
A basin headwall with multiple plausible lines and none of them obvious
The last 400 ft on the crest, steeper and more exposed than anything below and possibly low fifth class
A documented cliffing-out trap for parties drifting right below the summit
The North Ridge is not reversed on descent — the standard way down is the West Ridge, a different line

approach_variants.name: Elbow Lake Trail #697, the blue-blazed Green Creek path, and the moraine to the west ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. FR-38 is gated 1 December to 15 June for elk winter range, so this is a summer and autumn objective
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the north (Elbow Lake) trailhead via Mosquito Lake Road and Forest Road 38 — roughly 11 miles of gravel from the Mosquito Lake Road junction.

From the trailhead, Elbow Lake Trail #697 drops within a few minutes to the Middle Fork Nooksack River. There is no reliable bridge. The old log crossing washes out regularly, so expect either a ford — dangerous at high flow, best early on a cool morning when glacial melt is lowest — or an unofficial log or boulder crossing that may be up to a quarter mile off the main trail.

Once across, the trail climbs through old growth above the Green Creek valley, gaining about 1,000 ft over the first 3.5 miles toward the Bell Pass Trail junction.

Around 2,600 ft the maintained trail bends east into the Hildebrand Creek drainage. Leave it there, near a switchback, for the flagged Green Creek climbers' path with its small blue markers, which traverses south into the Green Creek cirque beneath Little Sister's northwest side.

Carry water for the ridge: Green Creek is the last reliable source.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SMALL BLUE DIAMOND MARKERS ARE THE WHOLE APPROACH, AND THE JUNCTION IS EASY TO WALK STRAIGHT PAST. Around 2,600 ft, near a switchback where Elbow Lake Trail #697 bends EAST into the Hildebrand Creek drainage, the unmaintained Green Creek climbers' path splits off. It is blazed with small blue diamonds. Every account says the same thing about it: look closely, because it is easy to miss. If the maintained trail has turned east and you are climbing toward Bell Pass, you have gone past it.

THE PATH ITSELF IS UNMAINTAINED, BRUSHY IN PLACES AND EASY TO LOSE IN FOG. Its direction is SOUTH into the Green Creek cirque. Blue markers going south is the confirmation.

THE UNSTABLE LATERAL MORAINE AT THE HEAD OF THE CIRQUE IS THE END OF THE APPROACH AND THE START OF THE ROUTE. Loose blocks, care needed, and the tread ends there. Above the moraine you gain the WEST RIDGE and follow it up through Class 2-3 talus and blocky olivine to the summit rocks, with short Class 3-4 steps near the top.

THE ROCK IS THE RANGE CHECK AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE: dunite, olivine-rich, famously high-friction — but loose in spots, which is a different thing from being unsound. Grippy where it is attached.

THE ROUTE-FINDING CRUX IS NOT AT THE BASE, IT IS IN THE UPPER THIRD, AND THIS IS WHAT THE FOG ACTUALLY COSTS YOU HERE: there are SEVERAL FALSE SUMMITS on the upper west ridge, and in poor visibility telling them apart is the hardest part of the day. There is no single marker for the true top; the honest advice is to note the shape of each bump as you pass it, because you will meet them again on the way down and the moraine and the unmarked path below are the things you have to find again.

WHICH PEAK AM I ON? Five summits share the Green Creek basin and the same climbers' path. LITTLE SISTER is the one dominating the SOUTHERN part of the cirque. CINDERELLA is reached from the low notch on the Cinderella-Little Sister ridge. SKOOKUM is further round the circuit. If you are at a col with a peak on each side, you are not on this route — this one goes straight up a ridge from the moraine.
hazards: A bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing whose log washes out regularly, worst at high flow
An unsigned, blue-blazed junction at ~2,600 ft that is easy to walk past
An unstable lateral moraine with loose blocks at the head of the cirque
Several false summits on the upper ridge and no maintained tread to return on
FR-38 gated 1 December to 15 June, and reported flood damage on the network

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier on its looker's-left side to the Cinderella-Little Sister col
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Green Creek one shared by every route on this peak: Elbow Lake Trailhead on FR-38, the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack crossing on whatever log is currently in place, then Elbow Lake Trail #697 and the blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' path leaving it near a switchback around 2,600 ft.

Up the Green Creek drainage past the Wiseman Lake outlet, through brush, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with Class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier.

This route then differs from its neighbours in one instruction: travel the glacier staying on the LOOKER'S-LEFT — south — side, up to the Cinderella-Little Sister col, which is where the ridge starts.

The route is graded around 5.3 and runs about three pitches.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A COL, AND THAT IS WHAT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM EVERY OTHER LINE ON THE PEAK. The southeast ridge starts at the CINDERELLA-LITTLE SISTER COL, at the head of the Green Creek Glacier. You have arrived when you are standing in a low point on a ridge with a peak at each end of it — Cinderella one way, Little Sister the other — and glacier behind you.

THE GLACIER INSTRUCTION IS THE ONE THING TO GET RIGHT AND IT IS A SIDE: stay LOOKER'S-LEFT, the SOUTH side, on the way up. The other routes on this peak do not go to the col at all, so drifting right across the glacier puts you under the north face instead.

SO THE DISCRIMINATOR IS SIMPLY WHETHER YOU REACHED A COL. If you have walked until the glacier runs into a WALL, you are at the north face and you are on a different, harder route. If you have walked until the glacier runs into a NOTCH you can walk through, you are at the start of this one.

THE MOAT AT THE GLACIER MARGIN IS THE LAST OBSTACLE, and it is a season problem rather than a route problem: trivial in a heavy snow year, a real step late in the season, and the same in reverse coming down.

WHAT NOT TO DO FROM THE COL, and it is recorded rather than inferred: do not continue along the connecting ridge toward Cinderella. At least one account describes that ridgeline as dangerously loose and recommends dropping back to the glacier instead. The col is a start point for two peaks and a through-route for neither.

DESCENT NOTE THAT DOUBLE-CHECKS THE START: most parties downclimb this same ridge back to the col. The alternative on record is to drop onto the NORTH FACE side and rappel scattered fixed pin and tat anchors back to the glacier — which is a different aspect and needs deciding on top, not in the moat.
hazards: A moat at the glacier margin that grows through the season
A dangerously loose connecting ridge toward Cinderella that must not be used as a traverse
Fixed pins and tat of unknown age on the north-face descent option
The bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing shared by every route here
Loose scree, boulder fields and Class 3 slabs to gain the glacier

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier straight to the foot of the wall, without going to the col
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Green Creek one: Elbow Lake Trailhead on FR-38, the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack crossing — the unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the marked ford is what most parties use — then off-trail to Green Creek, cross it, and ascend a rock buttress near 3,800 ft onto the Green Creek Glacier.

Where the Southeast Ridge continues to the Cinderella-Little Sister col at the glacier's head, this route stops at the face itself. It is graded around 5.4 and is the hardest of the peak's documented lines.

Descent is either rappelling the climber's-right side of the face on scattered fixed pin and tat anchors back to the glacier, or downclimbing the easier Southeast Ridge to the col and returning to the glacier from there.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GLACIER RUNS INTO A WALL, AND THE WALL IS THE ROUTE. That is the arrival and it is the whole test: walk up the Green Creek Glacier until the ice ends against rock that goes up rather than along. There is no col, no notch and no ledge system to identify.

THE COL IS THE OVERSHOOT MARKER AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING TO KNOW HERE. If you keep going and arrive at a low point on the ridge with Cinderella on the far side of it, you have walked past the north face and are at the base of the SOUTHEAST RIDGE — a different route, two grades easier, on a different aspect. Reaching a col means turn round.

THE ASPECT IS THE CONFIRMATION. This face is NORTH. It is in shade, it holds snow and ice at its base later than anything else on the peak, and the rock is cold. If you are standing in sun at the foot of your intended line, you are somewhere else on the mountain.

BE HONEST ABOUT WHAT IS PUBLISHED HERE: no source consulted gives a per-pitch start point along the base of this face. What is documented is the aspect, the grade, the approach glacier and the fact that the face is roughly a thousand feet high. A party arriving at the wall still has to choose its own line along the base, and should expect to.

DESCENT DECIDES THE DAY AND MUST BE DECIDED ON TOP: the two options are rappelling the climber's-RIGHT side of the face on scattered fixed pin and tat anchors — old gear, unknown age, treat it as found rather than as fixed — or downclimbing the Southeast Ridge to the col and back to the glacier that way. The second is more walking and less trusting.
hazards: No published line along the base of the face — the party chooses its own start
Scattered fixed pins and tat of unknown age as the rappel descent option
A north-facing wall that holds snow and ice at its base
A moat where the glacier meets the wall
The bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing shared by every route here

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit, then round onto the south side
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jan-May. This is a snow line and a winter ascent of it is on record; in deep winter parties have found hard snow all the way to the col
approach_variants.notes:
From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38, Elbow Lake Trail #697 reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack within a few minutes. THE BRIDGE IS GONE and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge to the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible at high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently there: one recorded party used a log roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction, another an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it and treat the crossing as the most consequential thing you do all day.

Once across, follow Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback near Hildebrand Creek, find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off up the Green Creek drainage, marked with small blue diamonds.

Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, up through the brush-filled valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with Class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. That is roughly five miles one way and 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead.

In deep winter, snowshoes have been left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL SOUTHEAST OF THE SUMMIT, AT 6,240 FT OR A LITTLE ABOVE, IS THE HINGE OF THE WHOLE ROUTE — AND THE COULOIR IS ON THE FAR SIDE OF IT. From the basin, climb snow to that col. Then TRAVERSE ONTO THE SOUTH SIDE and up into the gully. Nothing on the Green Creek side of the col is this route; you have to go over.

SO THE TEST IS AN ASPECT FLIP, WHICH IS THE MOST RELIABLE KIND IN CLOUD. You approach on the NORTH-facing Green Creek side, in shade, on the glacier. You climb on the SOUTH side, out of the basin you walked in through. If you are still looking at the glacier you came up, you have not crossed the col.

CONFIRM THE COL BY ITS NUMBER AND ITS POSITION: 6,240+ ft, and SOUTHEAST of the summit. A col northwest or west of the summit is the Cinderella-Little Sister ground and belongs to other routes.

WINTER CHANGES WHERE THE APPROACH ENDS, NOT WHERE THE ROUTE STARTS. In deep winter, hard snow has run continuously to the col, which makes the walk simpler and the col no less the marker.

BE CLEAR ABOUT THE RECORD ON THIS LINE, because it affects what you should expect to find: no rock or ice first ascent is recorded. What is documented is a ski descent of the line during a traverse of the range, and a party in January 2015 reporting a suspected first winter ascent of the peak by this south-side ground. It has been descended with more than 100 m of rappelling including a fixed final rappel requiring a knot pass. That is not a well-trodden route with a bootpack in it.
hazards: A bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing that must be hunted for and is the day's biggest consequence
A south-facing snow gully — timing matters and it warms
A line with no recorded climbing first ascent and very little traffic
Over 100 m of rappelling recorded on the descent, including a knot pass
Loose scree, boulder fields and Class 3 slabs to reach the glacier
